suggestions: Either accept this as concise foundational vaccine completion practice or require interpretation of a real product/history discrepancy before choosing the next dose.
Keep options clinically credible without the broad permission sentence or an explicitly redundant repeat-dose foil as the only active competitor.

review.title: Vaccine follow-up: MenB booster maintenance
clarityIssues: The record gives a 2021 booster but no encounter date or elapsed time since that dose. The filename/review date is not patient-visible clinical context, so 'overdue' is not established by the allowed visible fields.

cues.phrase: Give one booster of the previously used MenB brand
cues.why: The key is the reasonable intermediate action between restarting an explicitly adequate series and deferring all further doses. Neither distractor represents a credible competing booster interval.

fairness: A booster would be the best offered plan if the encounter is in 2026 as the artifact date suggests, but that date must not be silently imported into the clinical record.
The exact high-risk interval in the explanation was not independently verified offline. No confident contradictory clinical claim is made in this review.

Even once the date is supplied, this remains one booster-schedule rule rather than two consequential steps. The same-brand history does not require interpretation because all active dosing choices retain that brand.
Standalone case; no earlier node supplies the missing temporal anchor.
suggestions: Add a fixed encounter date or elapsed interval to the visible record so the question remains valid in frozen encounters and future play.
Compare plausible next-dose plans that require the history to distinguish primary completion from maintenance, or explicitly accept a focused basic booster item.
Do not create new intervals; use clinician-verified schedule details.

review.title: Preoperative vaccines: response after rituximab
fairness: This requires distinguishing apparently sufficient vaccine-to-operation lead time from impaired response after recent anti-B-cell treatment, then choosing later revaccination rather than accepting or immediately repeating the doses. Both timelines matter.
Planning indicated revaccination after recovery is the best offered answer. The wording 'indicated' appropriately avoids declaring that every prior dose always needs repeating.

The B-cell finding is legitimate decision-critical evidence, not a pre-answer statement that the administered doses are ineffective. The diagnosis of chronic ITP is appropriate background for the management task.

The exact post-rituximab interval and vaccine-specific revaccination rules require clinician confirmation; no fresh schedule verification was performed. Detectable B cells alone should not be construed as a complete validated measure of vaccine competence. The explanation's stated interval and reassessment language limit that overreading.
Standalone chronology is coherent. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified offline.
suggestions: Optional precision in feedback: clarify that reassessment combines the verified treatment interval, immune status and vaccine-specific guidance; do not make a single peripheral B-cell result an automatic revaccination or surgery trigger.
Retain the distinction between vaccine administration, operative lead time and expected response; it supplies the genuine reasoning.

review.title: Hospital record review: initial splenic abscess control
clarityIssues: The clinic presentation is retrospective, but 'should be recommended' sounds like a current treatment instruction. Explicitly identify the reviewed hospital decision point rather than leave the encounter's temporal perspective implicit.

cues.phrase: Which source-control plan
cues.why: The task preselects procedural source control while one choice is only continued antibiotic treatment. This removes a distractor by category and supplies the first management conclusion.

fairness: A single liquid unseptated collection with favorable access anatomy, persistent symptoms and substantial operative respiratory burden favors image-guided drainage among these choices.

Interpreting drainability and applying operative risk is a meaningful two-step comparison with splenectomy. The current antibiotic option, however, does not answer the same source-control task and is therefore weak.

The hospital record does not describe acute physiologic stability or rupture status. If either could alter the intended procedural ranking, add the relevant observed findings; do not assume the patient's later clinic attendance establishes prior hospital stability. This is a missing-context concern, not an assertion that this patient was unstable.
The explanation does not leak the later splenectomy choice and appropriately avoids a universal size threshold or guaranteed drainage success.
suggestions: Ask neutrally for the initial treatment plan at the specified hospital decision point, or compare three genuine procedural source-control approaches if three credible options exist.
Retain the anatomy and respiratory burden. Add only the observed acute safety information needed to make the chosen initial procedure unambiguous.
Keep the retrospective review frame short and consistent across both parts.

review.title: Hospital record review: persistent multifocal splenic infection
clarityIssues: 'Repeat image-guided drainage' is ambiguous between replacing a catheter in the collapsed original cavity and placing additional catheters into separate locules. These are clinically different actions.

The later update does not carry forward the home-oxygen requirement or prior prolonged postoperative ventilation. Those major competing operative risks appear only in the first exhibit, so this node is weaker when presented independently.
The retrospective clinic frame and 'should now be discussed' again leave the historical decision point less direct than it could be.

cues.phrase: Which source-control plan should now be discussed
cues.why: As in the first part, the task's category discounts the antibiotics-only option before the record is interpreted.

fairness: The changed imaging and ongoing bacteremia require a new inference: successful drainage of one cavity does not establish control of the remaining splenic infection. That is consequential and distinct from the first decision.

Splenectomy discussion is reasonable, but multiple separate locules without a dominant cavity do not by themselves establish that additional image-guided drainage is infeasible. The original substantial pulmonary risk makes that distinction especially important.

The item needs a supported patient-specific basis for ranking surgery over additional drainage. This is clinical ranking uncertainty, not a confident claim that splenectomy is wrong or that additional drains must work.

The chronology is otherwise coherent: the original catheter is patent and its cavity collapsed, then separate foci persist. Prior feedback cautions that drainage may fail but does not directly supply the surgical answer.
suggestions: Define the drainage alternative precisely and supply the observed access/anatomic or actual procedural findings that make it less appropriate in this patient. Do not replace that evidence with an unsupported blanket statement that multifocal disease cannot be drained.
Carry the relevant operative-risk history into the update so the later node stands alone and actually weighs the earlier competing consideration.
Use a neutral next-treatment task or only genuine source-control options, then have the clinician resolve the exact surgical-versus-additional-drainage ranking.

drafts.objective: Interpret an isolated platelet pattern and select missing secondary-cause testing before a primary-ITP label.
drafts.stem: Which investigation should complete the initial etiologic evaluation of {patientName}'s thrombocytopenia?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Counts and film
items.value: Platelets 55 x 10^9/L on two samples; hemoglobin and white-cell differential within reference ranges. Large platelets, no clumps or schistocytes.

items.label: Clinical review
items.value: No new medicine, lymphadenopathy or palpable organ enlargement. No mucosal bleeding.

items.label: Completed work
items.value: The referring team confirms that the two CBCs and manual blood films are the full diagnostic workup to date.

choices.label: HIV and hepatitis-C testing
choices.rationale: The isolated pattern still needs secondary-cause evaluation even without reported exposure risks.
choices.temptation: Treat a typical pattern as established primary ITP.
choices.counterfactual: With these tests complete and new lineage abnormalities, reassess for a marrow process.

choices.label: Marrow aspirate and biopsy
choices.rationale: Marrow can help atypical or refractory cases; it is not the missing routine initial study in this isolated pattern.
choices.temptation: Seek invasive diagnostic certainty before finishing etiologic screening.
choices.counterfactual: Dysplasia, another unexplained cytopenia or treatment failure would strengthen marrow reassessment.

choices.label: Platelet-specific antibody testing
choices.rationale: Routine antibody testing does not establish typical ITP and does not replace secondary-cause evaluation.
choices.temptation: Seek a confirming immune assay.
choices.counterfactual: Selected glycoprotein-specific assays may assist a difficult specialist diagnostic case.

drafts.explanation: The repeat count and smear support genuine isolated thrombocytopenia. HIV and hepatitis-C testing address secondary causes; a negative result still requires the clinical assessment before a primary-ITP diagnosis.

reasoningSteps: Interpret repeated nonclumping thrombocytopenia with other lineages preserved.
Select unresolved secondary-cause testing rather than invasive or antibody confirmation.
gate.closestError: Equate an isolated pattern with established primary ITP.
gate.decidingObservation: Compatible isolated counts/film and missing viral assessment.
gate.consequence: A secondary cause may be overlooked before surgical planning.
gate.cueAttack: All options are investigations. Neither a named virus nor an explicitly absent viral-testing category appears before the choice. The referring team confirms the actual completed workup, avoiding confusion between a missing export and an unperformed test.
gate.stageAndCategory: Initial etiologic investigation; three named test strategies.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: a more definitive-looking invasive test competes with baseline exclusion.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Viral testing wins. Add dysplasia and another cytopenia after complete viral testing and marrow reassessment becomes reasonable; a negative viral result alone does not force marrow.
gate.deletionTest: Count/film establish true isolated disease; test history establishes what remains. Removed generic follow-up permission.
gate.sequenceAudit: First node; feedback gives no later surgical calendar or treatment threshold.
gate.repairLog: Collapsed four cosmetic variants and removed the already-completed repeat-count foil. A later cue attack found that 'no viral serology' still named the key category; replaced it with confirmed performed-test history and re-solved the invasive competitor.

drafts.objective: Use duration, bleeding and count trajectory to avoid premature elective splenectomy.
drafts.update: HIV and hepatitis-C tests are negative; the broader assessment remains compatible with primary ITP. Five months have elapsed since diagnosis. Platelets remain 50-65 x 10^9/L, with no mucosal bleeding, anticoagulant use or upcoming invasive procedure.
drafts.stem: Which current treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s five-month ITP course?

choices.label: Continue hematology surveillance
choices.rationale: The early stable course supports observation rather than escalation to normalize the count or irreversible surgery.
choices.temptation: Treat persistence as the end of the nonsurgical window.
choices.counterfactual: A chronic course with important bleeding after adequate treatment failures can justify surgical evaluation.

choices.label: Schedule elective splenectomy
choices.rationale: The stable early course does not establish an elective operative indication; completing the diagnostic assessment does not change that calendar.
choices.temptation: Treat completed evaluation as an indication to operate.
choices.counterfactual: A selected chronic refractory case may proceed to vaccination and operative planning.

choices.label: Begin rituximab treatment
choices.rationale: The specified current course does not establish a need for medical escalation just to normalize platelets.
choices.temptation: Treat the abnormal count rather than current bleeding risk.
choices.counterfactual: Clinically consequential bleeding or another treatment indication changes the medical-treatment discussion.

drafts.explanation: Current bleeding and disease duration matter more than failure to normalize the count. Continue surveillance and defer elective splenectomy when feasible. A minimum deferral interval is not an automatic future operation date.

reasoningSteps: Interpret the trajectory as stable thrombocytopenia without a current escalation trigger.
Combine the early duration with that risk assessment to defer elective removal.
gate.closestError: Mistake persistence or completed viral testing for a surgical indication.
gate.decidingObservation: Five-month course without bleeding, anticoagulation or a procedure.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary medication or irreversible surgery may precede remission.
gate.cueAttack: Removed 'feasible medical care' from the old task. Necessary bleeding/procedure negatives establish surveillance; all choices are concrete current plans.
gate.stageAndCategory: Current treatment; surveillance, medical escalation and operative preparation.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: distinguish a treatment indication from a surgical calendar.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Surveillance wins. A longstanding course with recurrent important bleeding despite adequate therapies changes the elective discussion; bleeding alone does not mandate splenectomy.
gate.deletionTest: Delete duration and surgery may fit; delete bleeding/procedure context and observation is uncertain.
gate.sequenceAudit: Diagnostic feedback does not supply the calendar. New update supplies current facts rather than 'stable enough to defer.'
gate.repairLog: Removed repeated viral/marrow foils. Local lint found convergence of defer/splenectomy components; replaced the composite options with three parallel single treatment strategies and re-solved.

drafts.objective: Reconcile the missing vaccine and preserve its feasible preoperative interval.
drafts.stem: Which Hib-vaccination and operative schedule should be recommended for {patientName}'s elective splenectomy?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Operative plan
items.value: Splenectomy booked in five days for chronic medically refractory ITP. No current bleeding or urgent operative indication.

items.label: Vaccine record
items.value: Pneumococcal and meningococcal protection are current. Records confirm no Hib dose was administered.

items.label: Current treatment
items.value: No recent anti-B-cell treatment or other reason to expect an impaired vaccine response.

choices.label: Give Hib now; move surgery to at least 14 days afterward
choices.rationale: The missing adult dose and feasible preoperative interval both need correction.
choices.temptation: Complete the checklist without checking the calendar.
choices.counterfactual: A lifesaving urgent operation takes precedence over the preferred lead time.

choices.label: Give Hib now; keep surgery on the booked date
choices.rationale: Five days does not provide the preferred feasible interval for this elective case.
choices.temptation: Treat any preoperative dose as sufficient preparation.
choices.counterfactual: An urgent operation may precede the preferred interval.

choices.label: Give Hib after recovery; keep surgery on the booked date
choices.rationale: Postoperative delivery is a fallback when preoperative vaccination was missed; it is not preferred here.
choices.temptation: Use an emergency-operation pathway for an elective case.
choices.counterfactual: Unplanned urgent surgery with missed vaccines would use postoperative vaccination once stable.

choices.label: Give Hib after recovery; move surgery by at least 14 days
choices.rationale: Moving surgery while leaving vaccination until afterward creates no preoperative immune-preparation interval.
choices.temptation: Change the date but leave the preventive action unchanged.
choices.counterfactual: An unrelated medical reason could delay surgery, but would not correct this Hib plan.

drafts.explanation: Give the indicated adult Hib dose and allow at least 14 days before elective splenectomy when feasible. A booked date is not an urgent indication. Vaccine preparation also does not establish why the operation is needed.

reasoningSteps: Identify the documented unfilled Hib indication.
Apply the feasible preoperative interval to the booked date.
gate.closestError: Vaccinate correctly but operate too early.
gate.decidingObservation: No prior Hib, five-day booking and no urgency or B-cell depletion.
gate.consequence: The intended preoperative immune preparation may be incomplete.
gate.cueAttack: Four schedule combinations balance both components; the key is not the only choice that vaccinates or postpones. The task is an explicit scheduling comparison, so naming Hib is legitimate.
gate.stageAndCategory: One scheduling decision with parallel vaccine/date plans.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: knowing the vaccine is insufficient if the interval is misread.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Give now and reschedule wins. Change the record to urgent lifesaving surgery and preserving the operative date may fit.
gate.deletionTest: Each history/date/immune-response row sets a key boundary; no decorative preferences remain.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone elective case without prior teaching.
gate.repairLog: Replaced repeated organism-group recall with record and calendar interpretation; no gameplay wait duration in prose.

drafts.objective: Recognize when chronic treatment burden and multiple adequate medical failures support elective splenectomy evaluation.
drafts.stem: After control of the recent bleeding, which longer-term plan should be discussed with {patientName}?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Disease course
items.value: Primary ITP established three years ago. Recurrent mucosal bleeding has required repeated hospital rescue treatment.

items.label: Treatment record
items.value: Adequate hematologist-directed thrombopoietic-agent and rituximab courses failed to give a durable response; fostamatinib was stopped for intolerance. Prednisone responses were brief and caused substantial toxicity.

items.label: Current state
items.value: The recent bleeding has stopped after rescue treatment. The patient wants to avoid indefinite maintenance or repeated rescue treatment and accepts operative risks.

choices.label: Refer for elective splenectomy evaluation
choices.rationale: The chronic refractory course and informed preference support a hospital surgical discussion, without promising remission.
choices.temptation: Treat splenectomy as inappropriate after newer medicines exist.
choices.counterfactual: A recent diagnosis with stable counts and no important bleeding would favor deferring surgery.

choices.label: Restart prolonged prednisone maintenance treatment
choices.rationale: The documented brief response and toxicity make prolonged steroid maintenance a poor match to this course.
choices.temptation: Reuse a previously effective rescue response as a durable plan.
choices.counterfactual: A brief corticosteroid rescue course in an appropriate acute context is a different decision.

choices.label: Plan recurring IV immunoglobulin maintenance
choices.rationale: Recurring rescue therapy does not match the stated long-term goal after this chronic refractory course; it remains an interim option if surgery is unsuitable.
choices.temptation: Confuse control of the latest bleed with a satisfactory chronic strategy.
choices.counterfactual: Rescue treatment can bridge a new bleeding episode or an unresolved surgical contraindication.

drafts.explanation: Chronicity, adequate medical failures and treatment burden support discussing splenectomy with a hospital team. It offers a potential treatment-free response, with lasting infection and thrombosis risks; benefit is not guaranteed.

reasoningSteps: Distinguish temporary rescue control from failure of several chronic strategies.
Combine the longstanding course and informed treatment goal to select a surgical evaluation rather than repeated toxic or burdensome maintenance.
gate.closestError: Interpret a transient rescue response as adequate long-term control.
gate.decidingObservation: Three-year course, adequate failures/toxicity and a goal incompatible with indefinite rescue.
gate.consequence: Effective elective options may be deferred while treatment burden continues.
gate.cueAttack: Preference is necessary to rank a discussion against repeated rescue; removed generic 'good candidate' permission. Key is a named surgical referral, not generic shared decision-making.
gate.stageAndCategory: Elective management after bleeding control; three concrete treatment plans.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: distinguish indication for a discussion from a universal recommendation for surgery.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Surgical evaluation wins, not mandatory removal. Change to an early stable course or prohibitive operative risk and ongoing medical care becomes reasonable.
gate.deletionTest: Failure details distinguish rescue from durable response; the goal resolves a genuine plan tradeoff. Removed numeric success claims.
gate.sequenceAudit: First node. Feedback does not state how to interpret a negative accessory-tissue survey.
gate.repairLog: Used the 2026 guideline; no obsolete drug-ranking rule, precise dose or promised response rate.

drafts.objective: Avoid treating a negative preoperative survey as excluding tissue that could sustain hematologic disease.
drafts.update: At a later clinic chart review, the hospital team has selected elective splenectomy after counseling and preventive preparation. The current diagnostic review continues to support isolated ITP. Contrast CT identifies the spleen but no separate splenic nodule; the study is complete and technically adequate.
drafts.stem: Which next plan best fits {patientName}'s completed preoperative evaluation?

choices.label: Proceed with splenectomy and an operative accessory-tissue survey
choices.rationale: Negative imaging does not establish absence of accessory tissue; the selected operation still includes operative inspection.
choices.temptation: Trust imaging absence as proof of no additional tissue.
choices.counterfactual: New unexplained multilineage abnormalities would reopen diagnostic assessment before proceeding.

choices.label: Postpone splenectomy for another contrast CT survey
choices.rationale: Repeating a complete adequate anatomical survey does not remove its inability to exclude every accessory focus.
choices.temptation: Seek exclusion certainty by repeating an adequate study.
choices.counterfactual: An incomplete or technically inadequate first acquisition could justify completing appropriate imaging.

choices.label: Postpone splenectomy for renewed hematology diagnostic assessment
choices.rationale: The current review continues to support isolated ITP; this record supplies no new discordant finding to reopen the diagnostic premise.
choices.temptation: Treat a negative nodule survey as uncertainty about the platelet diagnosis.
choices.counterfactual: New unexplained anemia, leukocyte abnormalities or dysplasia would justify renewed diagnostic assessment without assuming a universal marrow-versus-flow ranking.

drafts.explanation: A negative CT is not a certificate that all accessory tissue is absent. For ITP splenectomy, inspect the hilum and other usual sites. The common-location fact does not define a complete operative search.

reasoningSteps: Interpret what a negative anatomical survey fails to exclude.
Apply the hematologic purpose of splenectomy to the operative exploration plan.
gate.closestError: Turn a common location or negative scan into search completeness.
gate.decidingObservation: ITP indication and no extra nodule on CT.
gate.consequence: Missed functioning tissue may contribute to persistent or recurrent disease.
gate.cueAttack: All labels are specific preoperative plans. The task does not name accessory-tissue search. A repeat study is plausible when acquisition is inadequate, and renewed diagnostic assessment is plausible when the hematologic pattern changes.
gate.stageAndCategory: Next preoperative plan; proceed with the selected operation or defer for a specified reassessment.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: distinguish a test's exclusion limit from either acquisition failure or a changed diagnostic premise.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Proceed with operative survey wins. Change the current isolated pattern to new unexplained anemia and dysplastic leukocytes and renewed hematology assessment wins; no marrow-versus-flow ranking is asserted.
gate.deletionTest: The adequate CT result and current isolated pattern resolve the offered reasons to delay. No image is promised: this tests report adequacy and exclusion limits, not visual recognition.
gate.sequenceAudit: Prior feedback concerns candidacy and risk, not search sites. Hospital selection is supplied only at this later stage.
gate.repairLog: Initial draft's counterfactual changed only initial search focus and failed to change the answer. Replaced its overlapping survey options, added acquisition/current-diagnosis boundaries, and re-solved a decision-changing counterfactual. New applied meaning; no history transfer from location recall.

drafts.objective: Distinguish improvement in synovitis from treatment of Felty-related neutropenia and infections.
drafts.stem: Which disease-modifying treatment change best addresses {patientName}'s current Felty-syndrome course?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Specialist assessment
items.value: Felty syndrome confirmed after hematology/rheumatology evaluation. Disease-modifying treatment has consisted of etanercept.

items.label: Treatment response
items.value: Etanercept has substantially improved joint pain and swelling. Persistent neutropenia and repeated skin infections have continued.

items.label: Today
items.value: No active infection. Creatinine and liver tests are within the laboratory reference ranges.

choices.label: Start specialist-monitored methotrexate treatment
choices.rationale: A joint response does not establish control of the neutropenia/infection phenotype; methotrexate is a usual initial disease-modifying treatment.
choices.temptation: Treat arthritis improvement as control of all Felty manifestations.
choices.counterfactual: An adequate failed methotrexate trial would require a different escalation discussion.

choices.label: Increase the current etanercept treatment
choices.rationale: The documented joint benefit has not controlled the infection/neutropenia problem; increasing the same arthritis-focused strategy does not address that distinction.
choices.temptation: Use the successful joint treatment as the next neutropenia treatment.
choices.counterfactual: Persistently active arthritis without this hematologic problem would be a different treatment target.

choices.label: Refer for elective splenectomy evaluation
choices.rationale: Medical treatment directed at Felty syndrome has not yet had an adequate initial trial.
choices.temptation: Use surgery to resolve the low count before disease-modifying therapy.
choices.counterfactual: Recurrent infections despite adequate specialist-directed medical therapy can support surgical consideration.

drafts.explanation: Assess the joint and hematologic responses separately. Methotrexate is a usual initial disease-modifying approach for Felty syndrome, with specialist laboratory monitoring. Evidence is limited; no dose or required trial duration is specified.

reasoningSteps: Recognize discordant joint and neutrophil/infection responses to the existing treatment.
Select the untried disease-modifying approach rather than equating joint improvement with full control or proceeding to surgery.
gate.closestError: Use synovitis improvement as evidence that the hematologic disease is controlled.
gate.decidingObservation: Joint improvement with continuing neutropenia/infections and no methotrexate trial.
gate.consequence: A preventable infection burden or premature operation may follow.
gate.cueAttack: The diagnosis is supplied because treatment, not syndrome naming, is scored. Eligibility observations are necessary for methotrexate; the text does not call it first-line.
gate.stageAndCategory: Current disease-modifying treatment plan; three specific strategies.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: competing organ responses, not the memorized triad.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Methotrexate wins. Replace the untried-treatment record with adequate medical failures and repeated serious infections and the surgical discussion changes.
gate.deletionTest: Response discordance makes increasing etanercept tempting; treatment history and organ function keep the choice fair.
gate.sequenceAudit: First node; feedback does not name an active-infection bridge or later surgical criterion.
gate.repairLog: Cue attack found an explicit missing-methotrexate sentence and an authored permission to use it. Replaced both with the actual treatment list and raw organ-function observations, then re-solved. Same first-line meaning; original approved variants stay exact.

drafts.objective: Choose rapid neutrophil support during active infection without using slower therapy or an infection-aggravating bridge.
drafts.update: A later clinic chart review concerns an outside-hospital admission for pneumonia. The hospital is administering antibiotics and supportive care. The neutrophil count remains markedly low.
drafts.stem: Which adjunct should be discussed for {patientName}'s neutropenia during the current pneumonia treatment?

choices.label: Begin filgrastim treatment
choices.rationale: G-CSF can support neutrophil recovery during infection while the hospital treats the infection itself.
choices.temptation: Treat a bridge as interchangeable with chronic disease modification.
choices.counterfactual: Without active infection and an urgent need for neutrophil support, the long-term disease-modifying plan is a separate decision.

choices.label: Begin high-dose prednisone
choices.rationale: Glucocorticoids may raise neutrophils but are generally avoided during active infection.
choices.temptation: Carry a possible noninfected bridge into an infected phase.
choices.counterfactual: A selected patient without active infection may receive a specialist-directed glucocorticoid bridge.

choices.label: Begin rituximab infusions
choices.rationale: A slower disease-modifying treatment is not the preferred acute neutrophil-support adjunct during this infection.
choices.temptation: Treat failure of chronic control as an instruction to start the next chronic agent during acute infection.
choices.counterfactual: After infection control, inadequate disease-modifying response may justify rituximab assessment.

drafts.explanation: The immediate objective is neutrophil support while the outside hospital treats pneumonia. Filgrastim can serve that bridge. Steroid and long-term disease-modifying decisions must account for the active infection and their different roles.

reasoningSteps: Distinguish active infection from a noninfected chronic-treatment visit.
Match the acute support objective to a rapid neutrophil bridge rather than an infection-aggravating or slower strategy.
gate.closestError: Choose glucocorticoids because they can raise the neutrophil count without accounting for pneumonia.
gate.decidingObservation: Active pneumonia with hospital antibiotics already in progress.
gate.consequence: An inappropriate adjunct may worsen infection or fail to provide the intended prompt support.
gate.cueAttack: Antibiotics are common background care rather than an option available only with the key. All alternatives are named adjuncts; no unsupported numeric target or dose.
gate.stageAndCategory: Acute adjunct during hospital infection treatment; three drug strategies.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate/hard; two plausible count-raising strategies diverge because of infection.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Filgrastim wins. In a noninfected bridge context glucocorticoids may become reasonable; chronic escalation after recovery is a different stage.
gate.deletionTest: Removing active infection destroys the steroid discriminator; removing existing antibiotic care makes the task unsafe.
gate.sequenceAudit: Earlier feedback gives chronic treatment, not this acute bridge. This is an outside-hospital record review in clinic, with no on-site inpatient service.
gate.repairLog: Removed a redundant team-request sentence that repeated the keyed rationale and changed the support-only key label to treatment. Re-solved the steroid competitor in active pneumonia. Single-source low-certainty limitation remains.

drafts.objective: Recognize clinically important failure of adequate medical therapy as the reason for a hospital splenectomy discussion.
drafts.update: At a subsequent clinic follow-up after infection recovery, the combined specialist record documents adequate methotrexate and rituximab treatment plus G-CSF support. Neutrophils rose briefly with G-CSF, but recurrent serious bacterial infections continued. No active infection is present today.
drafts.stem: Which next intervention should be discussed with the hospital team for {patientName}'s recurrent infections?

choices.label: Evaluate elective splenectomy
choices.rationale: Recurrent infections despite adequate medical treatment support multidisciplinary consideration, with no promise that surgery will prevent every infection.
choices.temptation: Judge treatment only by a transient count increase.
choices.counterfactual: Infection control on medical therapy would remove this refractory-infection rationale.

choices.label: Repeat the rituximab course
choices.rationale: An adequate course has not controlled the clinically important infection problem; another course is not the best-supported default from this record.
choices.temptation: Repeat a chronic regimen despite a documented unsuccessful clinical trajectory.
choices.counterfactual: A durable previous response followed by relapse could make retreatment reasonable.

choices.label: Start prolonged prednisone maintenance
choices.rationale: Prolonged steroid maintenance is not a preferred solution to this refractory infection course after adequate disease-modifying treatment.
choices.temptation: Translate transient neutrophil improvement into a durable infection-control strategy.
choices.counterfactual: A selected short bridge in a noninfected setting is a different role.

drafts.explanation: The deciding outcome is continuing serious infections despite adequate medical therapy, not a transient neutrophil increase. Hospital multidisciplinary splenectomy evaluation is reasonable. Lasting benefit is uncertain and preventive counseling remains necessary.

reasoningSteps: Interpret continued infections despite a transient laboratory response as inadequate clinical control.
Use the adequate treatment history and recovered care phase to consider an elective operation rather than repeat a failed or unsuitable chronic strategy.
gate.closestError: Call a treatment successful because a count briefly rose.
gate.decidingObservation: Recurrent serious infections after adequate methotrexate, rituximab and G-CSF, with current recovery.
gate.consequence: Ongoing infections may persist while a reasonable operative option is overlooked.
gate.cueAttack: Options are named interventions. Removed the old 'ineffective regimen without reassessment' caricature and transfusion-dependence foil. No success-rate promise.
gate.stageAndCategory: Post-recovery elective escalation; three concrete interventions.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate with low evidence certainty; independent clinician review must check the retreatment alternative.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Surgical evaluation wins in this constrained record. Durable infection control after medical therapy would favor continued medical follow-up; a new active infection changes the immediate stage.
gate.deletionTest: Adequate treatment and real infection outcomes determine the indication; current recovery separates elective evaluation from acute stabilization.
gate.sequenceAudit: Earlier feedback discusses disease modification and bridging, without teaching the refractory surgical criterion. Longitudinal updates are outside records, not elapsed gameplay months.
gate.repairLog: Retained the existing scored meaning and original approval. New exact application remains unapproved, without a mandatory-surgery assertion.

drafts.displayName: Acute production failure before HS surgery
drafts.objective: Interpret a suppressed reticulocyte response before using acute anemia to accelerate elective splenectomy.
drafts.stem: Which change to {patientName}'s elective splenectomy timing should be recommended from this hospital record?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Established course
items.value: Hereditary spherocytosis confirmed previously; elective surgical assessment was underway for chronic symptomatic anemia.

items.label: Before the illness
items.value: Hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL with a reticulocyte count of 12%.

items.label: Current hospital admission
items.value: After a febrile respiratory illness, hemoglobin fell to 5.9 g/dL and reticulocytes to 0.1%. Red-cell transfusion and evaluation are underway.

choices.label: Defer splenectomy pending production recovery
choices.rationale: The reticulocyte collapse points to an acute production problem; accelerating splenic removal does not correct that mechanism.
choices.temptation: Read the lowest hemoglobin as increased splenic destruction.
choices.counterfactual: After production recovery, persistently severe hemolysis and transfusion burden can support elective surgery.

choices.label: Advance the elective splenectomy date
choices.rationale: The abrupt reticulocyte suppression is not evidence that the spleen is newly destroying more cells.
choices.temptation: Use anemia severity without interpreting marrow response.
choices.counterfactual: Persistent severe hemolysis after the acute illness may justify renewed elective referral.

choices.label: Keep the scheduled elective splenectomy date
choices.rationale: An acute production crisis and current hospital evaluation need reassessment before preserving an elective calendar.
choices.temptation: Treat a pre-existing operative plan as fixed despite a changed mechanism.
choices.counterfactual: A recovered patient with stable operative preparation could retain a planned date.

drafts.explanation: The fall in reticulocytes identifies a different immediate mechanism from increased splenic red-cell destruction. Treat and evaluate the acute production crisis, then reassess the elective indication after recovery; the record does not establish a specific virus.

reasoningSteps: Interpret the abrupt reticulocyte fall despite worsening anemia as loss of production.
Avoid accelerating an elective intervention aimed at splenic destruction during the acute production problem.
gate.closestError: Use hemoglobin alone to infer a stronger splenectomy indication.
gate.decidingObservation: Reticulocytes fell from 12% to 0.1% after an intercurrent illness.
gate.consequence: An unnecessary or mistimed operation could fail to address the acute mechanism.
gate.cueAttack: No aplastic-crisis label or pathogen is supplied. All options are timing decisions, not a uniquely cautious test beside premature treatments; hospital stabilization is common background.
gate.stageAndCategory: Elective operation timing during an acute outside-hospital episode.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate/hard: interpret a changed production trajectory rather than apply the disease label.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Defer wins now. Restore production with persistent symptomatic hemolysis and the elective discussion can resume.
gate.deletionTest: The paired reticulocyte values determine mechanism; the prior indication makes continuing the planned date credible. Transfusion underway prevents an unsafe omission.
gate.sequenceAudit: First node; current record only. No future treatment response is exposed.
gate.repairLog: Separated acute anemia from the chronic operative indication; no exact crisis timeline, transfusion trigger or pathogen invented.

drafts.objective: Use recovered production, ongoing hemolysis and functional/transfusion burden to reconsider elective splenectomy.
drafts.update: At a later clinic chart review after the acute episode, the hospital confirms production has recovered. Hemoglobin repeatedly returns to 7-8 g/dL between transfusions; reticulocytes are 14%, indirect bilirubin remains elevated and haptoglobin is low. Repeated transfusions and exertional fatigue continue despite hematology-directed supportive care. The prior hereditary-spherocytosis diagnosis remains supported.
drafts.stem: Which longer-term intervention should be discussed for {patientName}'s continuing anemia and functional limitation?

choices.label: Referral for splenectomy assessment
choices.rationale: The persistent hemolytic course after production recovery carries an operative indication distinct from the acute crisis.
choices.temptation: Carry an acute deferral forward as a permanent prohibition.
choices.counterfactual: A compensated course with normal function and no transfusion need would favor observation.

choices.label: Scheduled red-cell transfusions as continuing treatment
choices.rationale: Transfusion remains supportive, but persistent burden and impairment justify discussing a splenic intervention rather than adopting support as the sole long-term strategy.
choices.temptation: Treat an effective temporary correction as an adequate durable plan.
choices.counterfactual: If surgery were contraindicated or declined, ongoing support would remain a legitimate plan.

choices.label: Glucocorticoid treatment for continuing hemolysis
choices.rationale: The record continues to support hereditary spherocytosis rather than a newly demonstrated immune hemolytic process.
choices.temptation: Apply an immune-hemolysis treatment to an established membrane disorder.
choices.counterfactual: A separately demonstrated immune hemolytic process would require a different treatment assessment.

drafts.explanation: After production recovery, the continuing reticulocytosis and biochemical hemolysis accompany substantial transfusion and functional burden. Discuss elective splenectomy with the hospital team. This does not rank total versus partial removal or promise a complete response.

reasoningSteps: Interpret restored reticulocytosis with low haptoglobin and elevated indirect bilirubin as continuing hemolysis rather than persistent aplasia.
Use the sustained transfusion and activity burden to reopen the elective surgical discussion.
gate.closestError: Treat the earlier deferral as a permanent decision, or mistake transfusion correction for disease control.
gate.decidingObservation: Production recovered but symptomatic hemolysis and transfusion dependence persist.
gate.consequence: A useful operation may be delayed while the burden of support continues.
gate.cueAttack: All choices are specific long-term interventions. Surgical referral remains a consideration, not an authored 'candidate' conclusion. No invented operation-response percentage.
gate.stageAndCategory: Long-term intervention after recovery.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: interpretation must be updated from the previous care phase; immune therapy is a secondary misconception.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Elective evaluation wins in this constrained course. With a compensated, asymptomatic course or operative contraindication, supportive follow-up becomes the better plan.
gate.deletionTest: Recovered production changes the previous answer; repeated burden gives severity clinical meaning. Removed spleen-size numbers that did not change the decision.
gate.sequenceAudit: Prior feedback requires reassessment after recovery but does not supply the later severity findings. Distinct current evidence changes the decision.
gate.repairLog: Kept total/partial selection unkeyed; no exact hemoglobin cutoff is claimed from the fictional values.

drafts.objective: Distinguish symptomatic biliary disease from a separate indication to remove the spleen in compensated HS.
drafts.stem: Which elective operation best fits {patientName}'s biliary symptoms and hematologic course?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Biliary course
items.value: Repeated postprandial right-upper-quadrant pain; ultrasound demonstrates mobile gallbladder stones without duct dilation.

items.label: HS course
items.value: Hemoglobin has remained near 12 g/dL for years. Mild reticulocytosis is unchanged. No transfusions, activity limitation or splenic pain.

items.label: Surgical assessment
items.value: The episodes have prompted an elective gallbladder operation discussion.

choices.label: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy
choices.rationale: The symptomatic gallbladder has an indication; the compensated HS course does not add an independent splenectomy indication.
choices.temptation: Assume any gallstone operation in HS should include the spleen.
choices.counterfactual: Severe symptomatic HS with a separate indication could support a combined surgical discussion.

choices.label: Cholecystectomy with total splenectomy
choices.rationale: The record does not establish a clinical splenic indication merely because the abdomen is being operated on.
choices.temptation: Use pigment-stone risk as a prophylactic total-splenectomy indication.
choices.counterfactual: Independently severe HS plus symptomatic gallstones can support concomitant treatment assessment.

choices.label: Cholecystectomy with partial splenectomy
choices.rationale: Retaining some spleen does not create an indication for an otherwise unneeded splenic operation.
choices.temptation: Try to solve an absent indication by making the operation smaller.
choices.counterfactual: Selected patients with an independent HS indication may discuss partial versus total options.

drafts.explanation: The gallbladder and spleen need separate indications. Symptomatic stones support cholecystectomy. The sustained compensated hematologic course does not establish a splenic indication, and this case does not decide total versus partial removal for a patient who actually needs it.

reasoningSteps: Interpret the stable functional/transfusion course as lacking a separate splenic indication.
Keep the operation directed at symptomatic biliary disease rather than automatically combine procedures.
gate.closestError: Add spleen surgery to every HS gallstone operation.
gate.decidingObservation: Years of compensated counts without transfusions, activity loss or splenic pain.
gate.consequence: An unnecessary irreversible splenic intervention could add lifelong risk.
gate.cueAttack: All options are operations. The shorter single-operation key is intrinsic to this comparison, not padded; no 'X alone' label. The full hematologic course is necessary to choose operation scope.
gate.stageAndCategory: Elective operative extent; three named operations.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: combined surgery is a credible convenience/recurrence trap.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Cholecystectomy wins. Severe persistent HS with independent functional/transfusion burden changes the combined-procedure discussion.
gate.deletionTest: The biliary findings establish one indication; the chronic HS course determines whether a second operation belongs. No unsupported stone-size threshold.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone case, no preceding severe-HS explanation.
gate.repairLog: Withheld asymptomatic-gallstone and total-versus-partial controversies; scored only whether a second indication exists.

drafts.objective: Interpret persistent spherocytes against corrected anemia and hemolysis before ordering a recurrent-disease workup.
drafts.stem: Which next plan best fits {patientName}'s current post-splenectomy findings?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Clinical course
items.value: Exercise tolerance restored after hospital splenectomy; no new fatigue, jaundice or transfusion requirement.

items.label: Laboratory response
items.value: Hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, reticulocytes and indirect bilirubin within the laboratory reference ranges.

items.label: Blood film
items.value: Spherocytes remain conspicuous. Howell-Jolly bodies are present.

choices.label: Continue planned hematologic surveillance
choices.rationale: Persistent morphology does not establish ongoing clinical failure when anemia and hemolysis have corrected.
choices.temptation: Require normalization of the inherited cell shape to accept clinical benefit.
choices.counterfactual: Recurrent anemia with biochemical hemolysis would reopen the diagnosis and residual-tissue assessment.

choices.label: Obtain abdominal CT for residual splenic tissue
choices.rationale: The current clinical and biochemical response does not supply the recurrence signal for a nodule-directed workup.
choices.temptation: Read a persistent smear abnormality as proof of retained spleen.
choices.counterfactual: Recurrent anemia and biochemical hemolysis could justify reassessment, including accessory tissue.

choices.label: Begin corticosteroid treatment for hemolysis
choices.rationale: The supplied response does not show current biochemical hemolysis or a new immune mechanism.
choices.temptation: Treat the cell-shape report as active hemolytic anemia.
choices.counterfactual: A new supported immune hemolytic process would be a separate treatment problem.

drafts.explanation: Splenectomy changes red-cell clearance, not the inherited membrane defect. Spherocytes can remain despite correction of anemia and biochemical hemolysis. Continue the planned hematologic follow-up; preventive care for asplenia also continues.

reasoningSteps: Interpret the discordant persistent smear and corrected clinical/biochemical course.
Choose follow-up rather than presume recurrent disease or start treatment without a current process.
gate.closestError: Equate persistent spherocytes with failed splenectomy.
gate.decidingObservation: Restored function, corrected anemia and normal reticulocyte/bilirubin values despite spherocytes.
gate.consequence: Unnecessary investigations or immunosuppression may follow.
gate.cueAttack: No 'successful operation' conclusion is supplied. Competing plans are specific; the test receives timing metadata even though wrong. Howell-Jolly bodies are a limited context clue, not proof of immune protection.
gate.stageAndCategory: Current follow-up plan after outside-hospital surgery.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: raw morphology can outweigh a coherent clinical response in a hurried reading.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Surveillance wins. Recurrent anemia with raised hemolysis markers changes the plan to reassessment; do not use absent/present Howell-Jolly bodies as the decisive test.
gate.deletionTest: Clinical recovery and biochemical response defeat the smear trap. The cell-shape observation supplies the consultation's reason.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone; no previous explanation announces the membrane-versus-clearance distinction.
gate.repairLog: Kept morphology interpretation separate from the frozen N3 nodule-function objective; no duplicate scintigraphy key.

drafts.objective: Recognize PIEZO1-associated dehydration as a different operative-risk disease from presumed HS.
drafts.stem: Which change to {patientName}'s proposed splenectomy plan is indicated by the new laboratory findings?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Referral label
items.value: Chronic familial hemolytic anemia has been treated as hereditary spherocytosis; splenectomy was proposed for ongoing symptoms.

items.label: Specialist red-cell laboratory
items.value: Few stomatocytes and no dominant spherocyte population. Osmotic-gradient ektacytometry shows a left-shifted dehydrated profile.

items.label: Molecular result
items.value: A pathogenic gain-of-function PIEZO1 variant is identified.

choices.label: Withdraw the splenectomy plan and return to hematology
choices.rationale: The new findings support hereditary xerocytosis, whose limited splenic benefit and thrombotic risk differ from HS.
choices.temptation: Treat familial hemolysis as a single surgically responsive category.
choices.counterfactual: A supported HS diagnosis with severe clinical burden would restore a different operative discussion.

choices.label: Proceed with the planned total splenectomy
choices.rationale: The diagnosis underpinning the proposed benefit has changed; the new disease carries a different risk balance.
choices.temptation: Carry the referral label forward despite new mechanism evidence.
choices.counterfactual: True severe HS after complete assessment may justify surgery.

choices.label: Replace total splenectomy with partial splenectomy
choices.rationale: A smaller operation does not establish an evidence-supported solution to this disease-specific contraindication.
choices.temptation: Reduce operative extent without resolving the wrong indication.
choices.counterfactual: Partial removal is a separate option in selected HS cases with a real indication; it is not a proved workaround here.

drafts.explanation: The genetic and dehydration findings redirect the diagnosis toward hereditary xerocytosis. Do not carry the presumed-HS splenectomy plan forward or assume partial removal neutralizes the different thrombotic risk. Return to specialist hematology planning.

reasoningSteps: Integrate the dehydration phenotype with a pathogenic PIEZO1 gain-of-function result to reject the referral's HS premise.
Apply the distinct benefit/risk of that disorder to stop the planned splenic operation.
gate.closestError: Preserve a surgical plan by changing extent while ignoring a changed disease mechanism.
gate.decidingObservation: PIEZO1 result plus a dehydrated, nonspherocytic phenotype.
gate.consequence: A poorly beneficial operation with a different thrombotic hazard may occur.
gate.cueAttack: The record does not print xerocytosis or contraindication. All options alter the same operative plan; total and partial remain credible reflex responses to symptomatic hemolysis.
gate.stageAndCategory: Revision of an existing operative plan.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate/hard: disease reclassification must change a previously plausible operation.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Withdraw the plan wins. A supported severe HS diagnosis changes the risk/benefit and supports a renewed operative discussion.
gate.deletionTest: The gene and phenotype must agree; symptoms establish why the initial proposal was plausible. No exact genetic variant or laboratory cutoff invented.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone clinic review of outside specialist testing; no additional diagnosis module or scored hematology companion required.
gate.repairLog: Avoided a generic all-stomatocytosis genotype claim; used PIEZO1 disease supported by the primary laboratory paper and current specialist guidance.

drafts.objective: Use the recorded conjugate product to distinguish completed vaccination from a remaining polysaccharide dose.
drafts.stem: Which pneumococcal vaccination plan fits {patientName}'s current record?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Risk history
items.value: Anatomic asplenia after splenectomy; no stem-cell transplant.

items.label: Registry record
items.value: PCV20 administered two years ago. No PPSV23 dose is recorded.

items.label: Current proposal
items.value: The referral asks whether PPSV23 is now due.

choices.label: Do not add a pneumococcal vaccine dose
choices.rationale: PCV20 is a completion endpoint under the checked guidance; asplenia does not by itself require adding PPSV23 afterward.
choices.temptation: Apply the older conjugate-plus-polysaccharide sequence to every conjugate product.
choices.counterfactual: A prior PCV15 dose without PPSV23 would leave a different completion requirement.

choices.label: Administer a PPSV23 dose at this visit
choices.rationale: The proposed additional polysaccharide dose is not indicated after the documented PCV20 endpoint.
choices.temptation: Treat absence of PPSV23 as proof of an incomplete sequence.
choices.counterfactual: After PCV15 without previous PPSV23 and an adequate interval, PPSV23 would complete the sequence.

choices.label: Administer a PCV15 dose at this visit
choices.rationale: A new lower-valency conjugate dose is not needed after PCV20 completion.
choices.temptation: Restart the conjugate pathway because the patient remains high risk.
choices.counterfactual: PCV15 is one option for an eligible adult without a prior qualifying conjugate vaccine, with the appropriate completion plan.

drafts.explanation: Read the actual product, not just 'pneumococcal vaccine.' The checked CDC guidance treats PCV20 or PCV21 as an endpoint without an added PPSV23 dose. Continuing asplenia risk does not mean every vaccine has the same booster rule.

reasoningSteps: Identify PCV20 as a different sequence endpoint from PCV15.
Apply that history-specific endpoint despite ongoing asplenia and an absent PPSV23 record.
gate.closestError: Use a universal conjugate-then-polysaccharide rule.
gate.decidingObservation: A documented PCV20 dose rather than PCV15.
gate.consequence: An unnecessary vaccine dose or repeated series may be arranged.
gate.cueAttack: Every option is a pneumococcal-dose plan. The question does not call the record complete. No generic 'individualize vaccination' key.
gate.stageAndCategory: Pneumococcal dose decision today.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate; product-history transfer error rather than organism-group recall.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: No extra dose wins. Change the recorded product to PCV15 without PPSV23 and an adequate interval and PPSV23 becomes appropriate.
gate.deletionTest: Product identity and prior polysaccharide history determine the branch; no unrelated vaccine checklist is included.
gate.sequenceAudit: First node. Feedback does not name which meningococcal serogroup is missing in the next update.
gate.repairLog: Used current 2026 product guidance, not outdated product paragraphs in the general immunocompetence chapter.

drafts.objective: Distinguish MenACWY coverage from a missing MenB primary course in an older asplenic adult.
drafts.update: The meningococcal registry review now shows an adequately completed MenACWY primary series and a recent MenACWY booster. No MenB doses have been given. The patient is 61 years old and remains asplenic.
drafts.stem: Which meningococcal vaccination plan should be recommended for {patientName} now?

choices.label: Begin the risk-based MenB primary series
choices.rationale: Asplenia creates a MenB indication beyond routine young-adult shared-decision ages, and MenACWY does not cover that serogroup.
choices.temptation: Treat age or a generic meningococcal record as eliminating the indication.
choices.counterfactual: A completed MenB primary course would shift the question to booster history.

choices.label: Repeat the completed MenACWY primary series
choices.rationale: Repeating the documented adequate series does not fill the missing serogroup-B coverage.
choices.temptation: Treat a second course of the recorded vaccine as broader coverage.
choices.counterfactual: A truly incomplete MenACWY primary course would require its appropriate completion.

choices.label: Defer further meningococcal vaccination this year
choices.rationale: The missing MenB course is a current risk-based indication rather than an age-limited routine choice.
choices.temptation: Apply routine healthy-young-adult age limits to asplenia.
choices.counterfactual: A fully current primary/booster record would allow deferring another dose until due.

drafts.explanation: MenACWY and MenB cover different serogroups. Asplenia supplies a risk-based MenB indication despite this patient's age; start the appropriate product-specific high-risk primary course. Prior documentation still matters for each vaccine.

reasoningSteps: Interpret an adequate MenACWY history as leaving serogroup-B coverage unresolved.
Use persistent asplenia rather than the routine healthy-adult age window to choose a MenB primary course.
gate.closestError: Treat all meningococcal products or age indications as interchangeable.
gate.decidingObservation: Adequate MenACWY, no MenB, ongoing asplenia at age 61.
gate.consequence: A consequential coverage gap can remain despite a 'meningococcal vaccinated' label.
gate.cueAttack: All options concern meningococcal vaccination; neither complaint nor task uniquely repeats MenB. No introductory statement tells the learner serogroup B is missing.
gate.stageAndCategory: Meningococcal vaccine course today.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: two common record/age errors compete.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: MenB initiation wins. Completed MenB with a due booster changes the action to maintenance rather than another primary series.
gate.deletionTest: The separate product histories and older age are necessary for the two competing errors.
gate.sequenceAudit: PCV feedback supplies no MenACWY/MenB rule. New registry information is revealed only in this update.
gate.repairLog: No exact primary-dose spacing invented; manager can link current schedule without hardcoding a clinical series into gameplay timing.

drafts.objective: Use the recorded conjugate product to distinguish completed vaccination from a remaining polysaccharide dose.
drafts.stem: Which pneumococcal vaccine action fits {patientName}'s current record?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Risk history
items.value: Asplenia after a nontraumatic splenectomy; no stem-cell transplant.

items.label: Immunization registry
items.value: PCV15 given two years ago. No PPSV23, PCV20 or PCV21 dose has been administered.

items.label: Current visit
items.value: No acute illness or vaccine contraindication. The patient asks whether the long interval means the series must restart.

choices.label: Administer PPSV23 at this visit
choices.rationale: The recorded PCV15 course has a remaining polysaccharide step, and the standard interval has already elapsed.
choices.temptation: Treat a long delay as invalidating the prior conjugate dose.
choices.counterfactual: Prior PCV20 or PCV21 would be a different endpoint without this added dose.

choices.label: Repeat PCV15 at this visit
choices.rationale: An extended interval does not require restarting the conjugate course.
choices.temptation: Convert delayed completion into a new primary start.
choices.counterfactual: A genuinely unvaccinated patient could start with PCV15 and an appropriate completion plan.

choices.label: Defer pneumococcal vaccination at this visit
choices.rationale: PCV15 does not carry the same endpoint as PCV20/21 in this history.
choices.temptation: Apply a newer conjugate endpoint to every product.
choices.counterfactual: A documented PCV20/21 dose would support no additional pneumococcal dose.

drafts.explanation: The prior product and the remaining dose determine the plan. PCV15 without PPSV23 remains incomplete in this record, and the interval is already adequate for PPSV23. A long gap does not itself require restarting vaccination.

reasoningSteps: Recognize a PCV15 sequence rather than a PCV20/21 endpoint.
Interpret the elapsed interval as permitting completion, not requiring a restart.
gate.closestError: Treat all conjugate products as complete or restart because completion was delayed.
gate.decidingObservation: PCV15 two years earlier, with no PPSV23 or higher-valency completion.
gate.consequence: An incomplete record may be mislabeled complete or extra doses added.
gate.cueAttack: Three concrete vaccine actions; no option is a generic cautious review. Counterpart PCV20 question is a separate case and must not be forced immediately before this one.
gate.stageAndCategory: Pneumococcal sequence completion today.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: apply a product-specific sequence to an interrupted record.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: PPSV23 wins among the offered actions. Change the prior product to PCV20/21 and no extra dose wins.
gate.deletionTest: The named product and elapsed interval determine the answer; the patient question supplies the competing restart error.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone variant of the same concept, not repeated scoring of one concept inside a paired case.
gate.repairLog: Local lint exposed convergence of dose/complete components. Replaced the labels with parallel single actions at this visit and re-solved both product-history branches. Same meaning across consequential variants, without a new FSRS construct.

drafts.objective: Distinguish maintenance boosting from restarting a complete primary course or ending risk-based vaccination.
drafts.stem: Which MenB vaccination plan fits {patientName}'s current high-risk follow-up?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Risk state
items.value: Anatomic asplenia remains. No recent immunosuppressive treatment.

items.label: MenB history
items.value: The same-brand high-risk primary series was adequately completed in 2020; a booster was administered in 2021. No MenB dose since then.

items.label: Other meningococcal vaccine
items.value: MenACWY booster history is current.

choices.label: Give one booster of the previously used MenB brand
choices.rationale: Ongoing risk calls for maintenance boosting; the long gap does not erase the adequate primary course.
choices.temptation: Treat an adequate primary series as lifelong protection.
choices.counterfactual: A current booster within its risk-based interval would permit deferral.

choices.label: Restart the full primary series with that MenB brand
choices.rationale: A delayed maintenance dose does not make the prior adequate primary course unperformed.
choices.temptation: Restart because follow-up was missed.
choices.counterfactual: A patient with no adequate primary course would require primary vaccination.

choices.label: Defer further MenB vaccination after the completed series
choices.rationale: The completed primary course does not end the ongoing high-risk booster indication.
choices.temptation: Apply a routine young-adult one-course model to permanent asplenia.
choices.counterfactual: A person without continuing high-risk indication may follow a different maintenance policy.

drafts.explanation: Under the checked CDC high-risk schedule, MenB boosting follows the primary series at one year and then every two to three years while risk persists. This patient is overdue for a same-brand booster, not a restarted primary course.

reasoningSteps: Interpret the record as an adequate primary course plus a lapsed maintenance interval.
Apply continuing asplenia risk to select a same-brand booster rather than restart or stop.
gate.closestError: Treat vaccine completion as permanent cessation or a gap as invalidation.
gate.decidingObservation: Adequate 2020 course, 2021 booster and continuing risk through the current 2026 visit.
gate.consequence: Risk-based follow-up may be lost or an unnecessary full course started.
gate.cueAttack: All options are MenB plans, and the task names MenB for all equally. Adequacy is necessary data, not the conclusion that a booster is due.
gate.stageAndCategory: One MenB dose/course decision today.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate; chronology and primary-versus-maintenance classification both matter.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: One booster wins. Make the last booster recent and deferral becomes appropriate; remove adequate primary-course evidence and primary completion must be assessed.
gate.deletionTest: Dates and course adequacy change the decision; MenACWY status prevents an unrelated simultaneous primary-series issue.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone patient; no prior MenB explanation supplies this key.
gate.repairLog: Used directly supported booster intervals; none is a gameplay testing wait.

drafts.objective: Recognize that documented non-live vaccine administration during B-cell depletion may not establish effective elective preparation.
drafts.stem: Which preoperative vaccination plan best fits {patientName}'s recent treatment record?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Operative context
items.value: Elective splenectomy is being considered for chronic ITP. No urgent indication is present.

items.label: Treatment chronology
items.value: Rituximab was completed two months ago; peripheral B cells remain depleted.

items.label: Vaccine chronology
items.value: Indicated pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccines were given last week. Surgery has been proposed three weeks after those doses.

choices.label: Plan indicated revaccination after B-cell recovery
choices.rationale: The ordinary preoperative lead time does not establish an adequate response during recent anti-B-cell treatment; reassess the doses and plan prevention after recovery.
choices.temptation: Count an administered non-live dose as proof of effective immunity.
choices.counterfactual: Without recent immune depletion, valid doses with adequate preoperative lead time can count toward preparation.

choices.label: Count the recent doses as completed preparation
choices.rationale: The calendar interval is not the only determinant; current B-cell depletion can blunt response.
choices.temptation: Use the two-week surgical interval without considering the treatment interval.
choices.counterfactual: Adequate immune response conditions without recent anti-B-cell therapy change this assessment.

choices.label: Repeat the same vaccines before the proposed operation
choices.rationale: A prompt repeat during persisting depletion does not resolve the response problem.
choices.temptation: Fix possible failed priming by repeating doses while the same mechanism persists.
choices.counterfactual: After recovery, indicated repeat doses may be planned under specialist guidance.

drafts.explanation: Separate administration, operative lead time and expected immune response. CDC advises waiting at least six months after anti-B-cell treatment for non-live vaccination, with some patients needing longer. Reassess the earlier doses and elective schedule with the treating team; recovery, not a new automatic operation date, governs the plan.

reasoningSteps: Recognize that recent B-cell depletion can undermine the response despite a non-live vaccine record.
Choose recovery-linked preventive planning rather than accept a calendar-only completion or repeat during the same depletion.
gate.closestError: Apply the preoperative two-week interval while ignoring the rituximab interval.
gate.decidingObservation: Rituximab two months ago and persistent B-cell depletion despite three-week operative lead time.
gate.consequence: A patient may undergo elective removal with ineffective intended immune preparation.
gate.cueAttack: Every option is a concrete vaccine plan, with no generic 'review with a specialist' label. The apparently adequate operation interval deliberately makes the accept-doses option credible.
gate.stageAndCategory: Preoperative vaccine-response planning.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate/hard: two independently relevant timelines must be separated.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Recovery-linked planning wins. Remove immune depletion and retain adequate valid dose timing, and counting the doses becomes reasonable.
gate.deletionTest: Both vaccine and rituximab chronologies are essential; current depletion prevents a calendar-only claim of recovery.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone clinic review of outside treatment records; earlier calendar item is not a mandatory companion.
gate.repairLog: No invented antibody-titer cutoff, automatic revaccination brand list or blanket live-vaccine ban. Specific repeat-dose decisions remain for Melissa and the treating team.

drafts.objective: Integrate liquid collection anatomy and operative burden when selecting initial splenic abscess source control.
drafts.stem: Which source-control plan should be recommended for {patientName}'s outside-hospital splenic abscess?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Infection record
items.value: Diagnostic aspiration yielded pus; the hospital has begun culture-directed antibiotics. Fever and left-upper-quadrant pain continue.

items.label: CT observations
items.value: One well-defined subcapsular splenic cavity contains liquid, without internal septations. It abuts the lateral abdominal wall; no bowel lies between the cavity and that wall.

items.label: Respiratory history
items.value: Severe obstructive lung disease requiring home oxygen. A previous abdominal operation required prolonged postoperative ventilation.

choices.label: Arrange image-guided percutaneous catheter drainage
choices.rationale: A solitary liquid cavity with this access anatomy supports a less invasive source-control approach, particularly with the documented operative respiratory burden.
choices.temptation: Treat every confirmed splenic abscess as an immediate splenectomy indication.
choices.counterfactual: Multiple separate or extensively septated collections would favor a different source-control discussion.

choices.label: Arrange hospital splenectomy for source control
choices.rationale: Splenectomy is a real source-control option, but the simple cavity and substantial operative burden favor an initial percutaneous attempt in this record.
choices.temptation: Choose the definitive operation without weighing collection anatomy and procedural burden.
choices.counterfactual: Multiple collections or a changed complex anatomy may favor operative source control.

choices.label: Continue culture-directed intravenous antibiotic treatment
choices.rationale: Continuing symptoms with an undrained liquid focus favor adding source control; changing neither drainage nor operation leaves that focus in place.
choices.temptation: Treat organism-directed drug selection as equivalent to controlling the infected focus.
choices.counterfactual: A clinical course without a remaining drainable focus and with infection resolution would shift the plan to medical follow-up.

drafts.explanation: Collection structure and procedural burden affect the initial source-control choice. The single liquid, unseptated cavity supports image-guided drainage while hospital antibiotics continue. This does not establish a universal size cutoff or prove that drainage always succeeds.

reasoningSteps: Interpret the CT description as a localized liquid collection rather than multiple separated foci.
Balance that anatomy and the respiratory operative burden to favor an initial percutaneous source-control attempt.
gate.closestError: Choose definitive splenectomy from the diagnosis while ignoring a suitable less invasive route.
gate.decidingObservation: One liquid unseptated cavity abutting the wall, plus a history of difficult postoperative ventilation.
gate.consequence: An unnecessarily burdensome operation or continued uncontrolled infected focus may follow.
gate.cueAttack: The record never calls the collection drainable or says interventional radiology is available immediately. CT access observations and respiratory history earn their roles in comparing real treatment plans. The shared antibiotic plan is not bundled uniquely with the key.
gate.stageAndCategory: Initial source-control strategy; three specific treatment plans at the outside hospital.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate/hard: surgery is a credible definitive competitor, but anatomy and operative burden favor a different initial approach.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Percutaneous drainage wins in this constrained record. Replace the single cavity with multiple separated collections throughout the spleen and operative source control becomes the stronger discussion.
gate.deletionTest: Delete cavity structure and drainage feasibility is uncertain; delete respiratory history and the initial percutaneous-versus-operative balance is less constrained. No exact size or antibiotic timeline is needed.
gate.sequenceAudit: First node is an outside-hospital chart review. Feedback gives no subsequent scan or promised clinical response; no ICU or interventional service is requested at the clinic.
gate.repairLog: Used current ICMR government guidance as the single adequate source. Excluded a candidate Cureus article after finding its explicit AI-use prohibition; no source prose, patient details, regimen or outcome from it used.

drafts.objective: Reassess source control when a drained dominant cavity does not represent the remaining multifocal infection.
drafts.update: A later outside-hospital entry records a patent catheter within the original cavity, which has collapsed around it. Fever, pain and bacteremia continue despite the directed antibiotics. Repeat CT now shows multiple separate thick-walled locules scattered through the splenic parenchyma rather than one remaining dominant liquid cavity. The founder is reviewing this new stage in clinic.
drafts.stem: Which source-control plan should now be discussed for {patientName}'s persistent splenic infection?

choices.label: Proceed with splenectomy
choices.rationale: The remaining infection is multifocal and no longer represented by the drained dominant cavity; the new anatomy favors operative source control despite the original procedural-risk concern.
choices.temptation: Treat an initially appropriate less invasive plan as a permanent commitment.
choices.counterfactual: A solitary residual liquid cavity with the catheter outside it would support renewed image-guided drainage instead.

choices.label: Repeat image-guided drainage
choices.rationale: Multiple separated locules with ongoing infection are a different source-control problem from the original solitary liquid cavity; the earlier rationale cannot simply be reapplied.
choices.temptation: Repeat a successful local intervention without checking whether its target represents the remaining disease.
choices.counterfactual: A single persisting liquid target inadequately reached by the first catheter could favor another percutaneous attempt.

choices.label: Continue intravenous antibiotics
