choices.rationale: The persistent clinical infection and changed collection anatomy require renewed source-control planning rather than retaining an unchanged strategy.
choices.temptation: Treat susceptibility-directed antibiotics as proof that source control has been achieved.
choices.counterfactual: Resolved infection with no remaining collection would support continued medical follow-up rather than a new operation.

drafts.explanation: Reassess what the catheter actually controls. Collapse of its original cavity does not establish control of separate infected locules elsewhere. Multifocal splenic collections with continuing infection favor hospital operative source-control discussion; respiratory risk still belongs in that planning.

reasoningSteps: Interpret a collapsed drained cavity alongside persisting bacteremia and multiple separate residual locules.
Change the source-control plan because the original local target no longer represents the current infection burden.
gate.closestError: Call source control adequate because the original cavity drained, or repeat the initial approach without reading the changed anatomy.
gate.decidingObservation: A patent catheter has controlled its cavity, but separate splenic locules and clinical infection remain.
gate.consequence: Persistent untreated infected foci may prolong systemic illness.
gate.cueAttack: The update gives catheter location, clinical trajectory and anatomical distribution, not the label drainage failure or an assertion that surgery is the only available service. The same three treatment categories remain credible across the two stages.
gate.stageAndCategory: Source-control reassessment after a distinct outside-hospital record update.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate/hard: resist both anchoring to the initially suitable plan and laboratory-only reassurance.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Operative discussion wins here. Change CT to a solitary residual liquid cavity not reached by the catheter and renewed image-guided drainage wins; no mandatory duration-to-failure rule is implied.
gate.deletionTest: The catheter's relation to the cavity prevents a simple malfunction assumption. The remaining locules and persistent infection change the choice; remove either and the operative ranking is less secure.
gate.sequenceAudit: Earlier feedback supports an initial attempt for a solitary cavity, not this later multifocal anatomy. Current-stage data are revealed only now; no patient is admitted to an in-game ICU.
gate.repairLog: Removed source-control wording unique to the key and made all three labels parallel treatment actions. Anatomy, rather than an invented number of antibiotic days, changes the decision. Single-source limitation and Melissa's review of the drainage competitor remain explicit.

answerChoices.label: Begin the risk-based MenB primary series

answerChoices.label: Defer further meningococcal vaccination this year

authorGate.closestError: Equate an isolated pattern with established primary ITP.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Compatible isolated counts/film and missing viral assessment.
authorGate.consequence: A secondary cause may be overlooked before surgical planning.
authorGate.cueAttack: All options are investigations. Neither a named virus nor an explicitly absent viral-testing category appears before the choice. The referring team confirms the actual completed workup, avoiding confusion between a missing export and an unperformed test.
authorGate.stageAndCategory: Initial etiologic investigation; three named test strategies.
authorGate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: a more definitive-looking invasive test competes with baseline exclusion.
authorGate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Viral testing wins. Add dysplasia and another cytopenia after complete viral testing and marrow reassessment becomes reasonable; a negative viral result alone does not force marrow.
authorGate.deletionTest: Count/film establish true isolated disease; test history establishes what remains. Removed generic follow-up permission.
authorGate.sequenceAudit: First node; feedback gives no later surgical calendar or treatment threshold.
authorGate.repairLog: Collapsed four cosmetic variants and removed the already-completed repeat-count foil. A later cue attack found that 'no viral serology' still named the key category; replaced it with confirmed performed-test history and re-solved the invasive competitor.

distractors.temptation: Seek invasive diagnostic certainty before finishing etiologic screening.
distractors.counterfactual: Dysplasia, another unexplained cytopenia or treatment failure would strengthen marrow reassessment.

items.label: Operative plan
items.value: Splenectomy booked in five days for chronic medically refractory ITP. No current bleeding or urgent operative indication.

items.label: Vaccine record
items.value: Pneumococcal and meningococcal protection are current. Records confirm no Hib dose was administered.

items.label: Current treatment
items.value: No recent anti-B-cell treatment or other reason to expect an impaired vaccine response.

answerChoices.label: Give Hib now; move surgery to at least 14 days afterward
answerChoices.rationale: The missing adult dose and feasible preoperative interval both need correction.

answerChoices.label: Give Hib now; keep surgery on the booked date
answerChoices.rationale: Five days does not provide the preferred feasible interval for this elective case.

answerChoices.label: Give Hib after recovery; keep surgery on the booked date
answerChoices.rationale: Postoperative delivery is a fallback when preoperative vaccination was missed; it is not preferred here.

answerChoices.label: Give Hib after recovery; move surgery by at least 14 days
answerChoices.rationale: Moving surgery while leaving vaccination until afterward creates no preoperative immune-preparation interval.

node.explanation: Give the indicated adult Hib dose and allow at least 14 days before elective splenectomy when feasible. A booked date is not an urgent indication. Vaccine preparation also does not establish why the operation is needed.
sourceLabels: Adult Immunization Schedule Notes, United States, 2025 (2025)

distractors.label: Give Hib now; keep surgery on the booked date
distractors.rationale: Five days does not provide the preferred feasible interval for this elective case.
distractors.temptation: Treat any preoperative dose as sufficient preparation.
distractors.counterfactual: An urgent operation may precede the preferred interval.

distractors.label: Give Hib after recovery; keep surgery on the booked date
distractors.rationale: Postoperative delivery is a fallback when preoperative vaccination was missed; it is not preferred here.
distractors.temptation: Use an emergency-operation pathway for an elective case.
distractors.counterfactual: Unplanned urgent surgery with missed vaccines would use postoperative vaccination once stable.

distractors.temptation: Change the date but leave the preventive action unchanged.
distractors.counterfactual: An unrelated medical reason could delay surgery, but would not correct this Hib plan.

question.stem: After control of the recent bleeding, which longer-term plan should be discussed with {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Refer for elective splenectomy evaluation
answerChoices.rationale: The chronic refractory course and informed preference support a hospital surgical discussion, without promising remission.

answerChoices.label: Restart prolonged prednisone maintenance treatment
answerChoices.rationale: The documented brief response and toxicity make prolonged steroid maintenance a poor match to this course.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The documented brief response and toxicity make prolonged steroid maintenance a poor match to this course.

answerChoices.label: Plan recurring IV immunoglobulin maintenance
answerChoices.rationale: Recurring rescue therapy does not match the stated long-term goal after this chronic refractory course; it remains an interim option if surgery is unsuitable.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Recurring rescue therapy does not match the stated long-term goal after this chronic refractory course; it remains an interim option if surgery is unsuitable.

question.explanation: Chronicity, adequate medical failures and treatment burden support discussing splenectomy with a hospital team. It offers a potential treatment-free response, with lasting infection and thrombosis risks; benefit is not guaranteed.

items.label: Treatment record
items.value: Adequate hematologist-directed thrombopoietic-agent and rituximab courses failed to give a durable response; fostamatinib was stopped for intolerance. Prednisone responses were brief and caused substantial toxicity.

items.label: Current state
items.value: The recent bleeding has stopped after rescue treatment. The patient wants to avoid indefinite maintenance or repeated rescue treatment and accepts operative risks.

question.stem: Which next plan best fits {patientName}'s completed preoperative evaluation?

answerChoices.label: Proceed with splenectomy and an operative accessory-tissue survey
answerChoices.rationale: Negative imaging does not establish absence of accessory tissue; the selected operation still includes operative inspection.

answerChoices.label: Postpone splenectomy for another contrast CT survey
answerChoices.rationale: Repeating a complete adequate anatomical survey does not remove its inability to exclude every accessory focus.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeating a complete adequate anatomical survey does not remove its inability to exclude every accessory focus.

answerChoices.label: Postpone splenectomy for renewed hematology diagnostic assessment
answerChoices.rationale: The current review continues to support isolated ITP; this record supplies no new discordant finding to reopen the diagnostic premise.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The current review continues to support isolated ITP; this record supplies no new discordant finding to reopen the diagnostic premise.

question.explanation: A negative CT is not a certificate that all accessory tissue is absent. For ITP splenectomy, inspect the hilum and other usual sites. The common-location fact does not define a complete operative search.

question.stem: Which disease-modifying treatment change best addresses {patientName}'s current Felty-syndrome course?

answerChoices.label: Start specialist-monitored methotrexate treatment
answerChoices.rationale: A joint response does not establish control of the neutropenia/infection phenotype; methotrexate is a usual initial disease-modifying treatment.

answerChoices.label: Increase the current etanercept treatment
answerChoices.rationale: The documented joint benefit has not controlled the infection/neutropenia problem; increasing the same arthritis-focused strategy does not address that distinction.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The documented joint benefit has not controlled the infection/neutropenia problem; increasing the same arthritis-focused strategy does not address that distinction.

answerChoices.label: Refer for elective splenectomy evaluation
answerChoices.rationale: Medical treatment directed at Felty syndrome has not yet had an adequate initial trial.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Medical treatment directed at Felty syndrome has not yet had an adequate initial trial.

question.explanation: Assess the joint and hematologic responses separately. Methotrexate is a usual initial disease-modifying approach for Felty syndrome, with specialist laboratory monitoring. Evidence is limited; no dose or required trial duration is specified.

question.stem: Which adjunct should be discussed for {patientName}'s neutropenia during the current pneumonia treatment?

answerChoices.label: Begin filgrastim treatment
answerChoices.rationale: G-CSF can support neutrophil recovery during infection while the hospital treats the infection itself.

answerChoices.label: Begin high-dose prednisone
answerChoices.rationale: Glucocorticoids may raise neutrophils but are generally avoided during active infection.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Glucocorticoids may raise neutrophils but are generally avoided during active infection.

answerChoices.label: Begin rituximab infusions
answerChoices.rationale: A slower disease-modifying treatment is not the preferred acute neutrophil-support adjunct during this infection.

manualDispositions.disposition: Investigation category warning is lexical (all three are investigations); HIV abbreviation is a standard test name, not a visible diagnosis or a unique pre-answer test. Explicit absent-viral-test category was removed.

The single indicated operation is intrinsically shorter than each two-operation plan. Keep the clinically meaningful extent comparison without padding or an X-alone label; independent reviewer must assess this residual length cue.
Pneumococcal/vaccine words name the common category. The absent PPSV23 record is necessary: the error is treating that absence as incompleteness despite PCV20. Do not remove the product history.
The actual MenB and MenACWY histories are necessary evidence; no authored statement says coverage is incomplete or applies the age rule for the learner. Retain record-level product names.
The direct product names are necessary for this history-specific decision. Repaired dose/complete component convergence with three parallel current actions; no majority-component shortcut retained.
Prior booster history determines maintenance timing; the chief complaint was changed from Booster review to Vaccine follow-up. The past dose does not announce that another is currently due.

Generic after/indicated word matches have no clinical option-elimination force. Treatment and vaccine chronologies, plus current B-cell depletion, earn their place; no unique revaccination permission.

claims.statement: Initial ITP evaluation uses history, examination, blood count and expert smear; a compatible isolated pattern does not require routine diagnostic marrow sampling.
claims.limitation: One adequate diagnostic consensus. Atypical features, treatment failure or surgical reassessment may justify marrow assessment.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: HIV and hepatitis-C testing help identify secondary causes in suspected adult ITP even without reported exposure risks.
claims.limitation: One adequate diagnostic consensus. Negative tests neither establish primary ITP nor mandate marrow sampling.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: Routine platelet-antibody testing is not the principal diagnostic confirmation for typical ITP; selected assays may assist difficult specialist cases.
claims.limitation: One consensus publication; no assay performance numbers taught.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: When clinically feasible, elective ITP splenectomy is deferred at least one year after diagnosis because remission remains possible.
claims.limitation: ASH 2026 feasible-delay good-practice statement; 2019 consensus suggests 12-24 months. Neither mandates surgery at one year.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: Observation may suit an otherwise stable adult with platelet counts at least 30 x 10^9/L and absent or minor bleeding after considering additional bleeding risks and planned procedures.
claims.limitation: Current publication retains older treatment threshold. Constructed patient values are not new cutoffs.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: Splenectomy can be considered in chronic primary ITP after failure or intolerance of multiple adequate medical therapies or when avoiding chronic medication is a major goal.
claims.limitation: Consideration, not universal superiority or guaranteed remission.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: Indicated pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccines are coordinated at least 14 days before elective splenectomy when feasible.
claims.limitation: Not a reason to delay lifesaving surgery; not all vaccine series finish in this interval.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: An adult with anatomic or functional asplenia who has not previously received Hib vaccine is recommended one Hib dose.
claims.limitation: One federal authority. HSCT revaccination is a different pathway.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: An adult who has received PCV20 or PCV21 does not routinely receive an additional pneumococcal vaccine dose under the checked CDC guidance.
claims.limitation: Two CDC pages are one authority; recheck at publication.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: PCV15 in an adult without prior PPSV23 is normally followed by PPSV23 at least one year later; selected risk states permit a shorter minimum.
claims.limitation: Case is well beyond the standard interval and does not test the shorter exception. One authority.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: MenACWY does not supply serogroup-B coverage; asplenia creates a risk-based MenB indication beyond routine young-adult shared-decision ages.
claims.limitation: One federal authority; product/history determine the high-risk primary series.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: With ongoing high risk, CDC recommends a MenB booster one year after the primary series and further boosters every two to three years.
claims.limitation: One authority. Same brand; do not restart an adequate series.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: Anti-B-cell therapy impairs non-live vaccine response; CDC advises waiting at least six months after treatment, sometimes longer depending on recovery.
claims.limitation: Does not imply non-live vaccines are intrinsically unsafe, or prescribe a repeat rituximab course.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: Aplastic crisis can abruptly worsen hereditary-spherocytosis anemia; a falling reticulocyte response indicates impaired production rather than simply increased splenic red-cell destruction.
claims.limitation: One current specialist guideline. Constructed reticulocyte values are not cutoffs and do not prove a pathogen.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: Hereditary-spherocytosis splenectomy decisions depend on persistent clinical severity, transfusion burden and functional impairment, not one acute low hemoglobin.
claims.limitation: Adult decisions use specialist guidance; cross-check cohort is pediatric. Operation type not ranked.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: Symptomatic gallstones support cholecystectomy in hereditary spherocytosis; an otherwise compensated splenic course does not acquire a separate splenectomy indication from gallstones alone.
claims.limitation: No asymptomatic-gallbladder prophylactic operation ranking.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: Splenectomy may correct hereditary-spherocytosis anemia and biochemical hemolysis while abnormal red-cell morphology persists because the membrane defect remains.
claims.limitation: One current specialist guideline; smear is not a substitute for clinical response.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: Negative preoperative accessory-spleen imaging does not remove the need for operative inspection for accessory tissue during ITP splenectomy.
claims.limitation: Expert-opinion surgical guidance; no sensitivity or search-completeness percentage asserted.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: Methotrexate is a usual initial disease-modifying treatment for Felty syndrome; arthritis control by a TNF inhibitor does not establish control of neutropenia and infections.
claims.limitation: One adequate open synthesis; underlying reports/series are limited. No dose or required duration authored.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: G-CSF can improve neutrophils during active infection in Felty syndrome; glucocorticoids are generally avoided during infection and disease-modifying agents act more slowly.
claims.limitation: One adequate open synthesis. Hospital infection treatment is already underway; no G-CSF dose or ANC target taught.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: Splenectomy is an option to consider for Felty syndrome with recurrent infections despite adequate medical treatment; durable infection control is not guaranteed.
claims.limitation: One open synthesis with heterogeneous historical evidence; hospital multidisciplinary consideration, not a mandatory operation.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: Pathogenic gain-of-function PIEZO1 variants can produce hereditary xerocytosis with red-cell dehydration and chronic hemolysis.
claims.limitation: No exact mutation, laboratory cutoff or genotype severity prediction invented.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: Splenectomy is avoided in hereditary xerocytosis because limited hematologic benefit and thrombotic risk differ from the usual hereditary-spherocytosis balance.
claims.limitation: Guideline supports management; primary study cross-checks identity and thrombotic association.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: Splenectomy carries lasting infection and thrombosis risks; preventive vaccination and education about fever remain relevant after hematologic improvement.
claims.limitation: General preventive boundary, not an exact antibiotic regimen, prophylaxis duration or measured risk estimate.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults matching the constrained splenic-disease or asplenia case, not every hematologic disorder.

claims.statement: A liquid unilocular or bilocular splenic abscess without internal septations can be suitable for percutaneous drainage; its less invasive burden can matter when operative risk is high.
claims.limitation: One adequate government guidance source. No clinical success percentage, numeric size cutoff, antibiotic regimen or required trial duration inferred. Specific operative choice needs clinician review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with confirmed nontraumatic pyogenic splenic abscess in an outside hospital; the clinic reviews the record.

claims.statement: Multiple splenic abscess collections can favor operative source control rather than percutaneous drainage; treatment selection depends on collection anatomy, not size alone.
claims.limitation: One adequate government guidance source. No clinical success percentage, numeric size cutoff, antibiotic regimen or required trial duration inferred. Specific operative choice needs clinician review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with confirmed nontraumatic pyogenic splenic abscess in an outside hospital; the clinic reviews the record.

claims.statement: The splenic hilum is the most common location represented for an accessory spleen in this approved anatomy concept.
claims.limitation: The package intentionally omits an exact prevalence estimate and does not turn this common-location teaching point into a complete operative search rule.
claims.applicablePopulation: Patients represented by the approved clinic discussions surrounding referral for hospital splenectomy.

claims.statement: A common accessory-spleen location does not establish that inspection of that one location alone is sufficient during splenectomy.
claims.limitation: This concept does not address retained accessory tissue, recurrent hemolysis, completion splenectomy, reoperation, or any operative-management sequence.
claims.applicablePopulation: Learners applying the narrow location-recognition concept rather than an operative-management protocol.

claims.statement: Before elective splenectomy, indicated pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Hib vaccines should be reviewed and given at least 14 days before surgery when possible.
claims.limitation: This does not reproduce product schedules or delay an urgent operation.
claims.applicablePopulation: Stable adults preparing for elective splenectomy.

claims.statement: Fever in a person with impaired splenic function requires immediate emergency assessment; a patient-specific standby oral antibiotic plan does not replace emergency presentation or prompt parenteral treatment after evaluation.
claims.limitation: The case does not select a drug, dose, diagnosis, or outpatient test pathway.
claims.applicablePopulation: Known asplenic adults with new fever.

claims.statement: Felty syndrome is suggested by long-standing, usually seropositive rheumatoid arthritis with persistent neutropenia; splenomegaly is a characteristic supporting feature and recurrent infections may be the presenting problem.
claims.limitation: The pattern is not pathognomonic. The approved diagnostic vignette explicitly excludes medication, infection, and clonal large-granular-lymphocyte causes before asking for the syndrome.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with established rheumatoid arthritis and persistent otherwise-unexplained neutropenia.

claims.statement: Splenomegaly is common in Felty syndrome but is not an absolute prerequisite; persistent neutropenia in the appropriate rheumatoid-arthritis context remains the essential hematologic feature.
claims.limitation: A normal-sized spleen does not establish Felty syndrome and does not remove the need to investigate alternative causes of neutropenia.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with rheumatoid arthritis and persistent neutropenia after alternative causes have been evaluated.

claims.statement: T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia and other hematologic, infectious, autoimmune, and medication-related causes can resemble Felty syndrome and require explicit exclusion rather than diagnosis from the triad alone.
claims.limitation: This package does not teach the complete hematologic workup or a separate T-LGL diagnosis concept.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with rheumatoid arthritis, neutropenia, and possible splenomegaly undergoing diagnostic evaluation.

claims.statement: Methotrexate is the usual first-line disease-modifying treatment for confirmed Felty syndrome when treatment is indicated, with specialist monitoring of blood counts and clinical response.
claims.limitation: Felty syndrome is rare and treatment evidence is based mainly on case reports and small case series rather than randomized trials; this concept does not prescribe a dose or monitoring interval.
claims.applicablePopulation: Stable adults with confirmed Felty syndrome who do not have an active infection and have not yet received syndrome-directed disease-modifying treatment.

claims.statement: Glucocorticoids or G-CSF may be used as temporary bridging or supportive therapy while disease-modifying treatment takes effect; glucocorticoids are not universally contraindicated but should be avoided in active infection and are not the preferred sole long-term strategy.
claims.limitation: The approved questions do not prescribe a dose, duration, laboratory target, or universal bridging regimen.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with confirmed Felty syndrome receiving specialist-directed treatment.

claims.statement: Splenectomy is generally reserved for Felty syndrome with recurrent infections despite adequate medical treatment rather than used as routine initial therapy.
claims.limitation: The exact likelihood and durability of hematologic response are not taught because the evidence is old, heterogeneous, and confounded by historical overlap with T-LGL leukemia.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with confirmed Felty syndrome and recurrent infections despite adequate specialist-directed medical therapy.

claims.statement: For the approved presentation of persistent anemia with biochemical hemolysis after documented total splenectomy, reassessment and evaluation for accessory splenic tissue is the selected next step.
claims.limitation: MCV or RDW alone does not establish persistent hemolysis, and this narrow teaching path does not diagnose every cause of anemia after splenectomy.
claims.applicablePopulation: Patients matching the approved hereditary-spherocytosis post-splenectomy presentations.

claims.statement: Absent Howell-Jolly bodies after splenectomy can support suspicion of residual functioning splenic tissue.

revisionDrafts.objective: Use duration, bleeding and count trajectory to avoid premature elective splenectomy.
revisionDrafts.stem: Which treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s current ITP course?

choices.label: Continue weekly romiplostim treatment
choices.rationale: The observed response is treatment-dependent, so stopping support is different from observing a remission. Effective current support makes deferral during the first disease year feasible.
choices.temptation: Mistake a safe count on treatment for untreated remission.
choices.counterfactual: If counts and bleeding remained controlled after treatment withdrawal, medication-free surveillance could become appropriate.

choices.label: Schedule elective splenectomy after preparation
choices.rationale: Avoiding maintenance can support later splenectomy consideration, but the five-month course and effective bridge favor deferral now.
choices.temptation: Treat a preference for finite treatment as requiring immediate elective surgery.
choices.counterfactual: With a chronic course beyond the recommended deferral period and a continuing informed preference against maintenance, elective splenectomy discussion could become the favored offered plan; duration alone would not mandate it.

choices.label: Withdraw romiplostim with platelet surveillance
choices.rationale: The interruption was followed by recurrent bleeding and a falling count. The current count does not demonstrate medication-free disease control.
choices.temptation: Treat the current response as spontaneous remission.
choices.counterfactual: Durable safe counts and absence of bleeding after withdrawal would support deferring both the medicine and the operation.

revisionDrafts.explanation: The count rose with treatment, fell with interruption and rose again after resumption. That course supports maintaining an effective bridge rather than assuming remission. At five months, feasible elective splenectomy deferral still matters despite the longer-term wish to avoid maintenance. Reassess the preference and disease course later; a calendar anniversary does not itself establish an operative indication.

reasoningSteps: Interpret the interruption/resumption record as treatment-dependent platelet control rather than untreated remission.
Use that effective bridge and the five-month disease duration to defer elective splenectomy while continuing support.
gate.closestError: The nearest competitor continues the same effective medicine but schedules surgery now because the patient ultimately wants finite treatment.
gate.decidingObservation: Control is lost off treatment, yet restored with it; the disease is only five months old and the patient accepts temporary continued support.
gate.consequence: An incorrect plan would expose this patient to an unnecessary intervention or defer indicated protection or disease-directed assessment.
gate.cueAttack: Three parallel current management actions: maintain treatment, schedule an operation, or withdraw treatment. Removed the three-way paired medication/operation matrix after the component-frequency attack showed that the key combined two majority components. Both treatment continuation and withdrawal remain plausible until the response record is read.
gate.stageAndCategory: One current decision stage: specific management plans with comparable scope; patient observations and rationale remain separated.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate; author estimate only, pending independent re-review. The nearest competitor is identified below rather than using rarity to claim difficulty.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Continue treatment and defer surgery here. Change the five-month history to established chronic disease beyond the feasible deferral period with an informed persistent goal against maintenance, and the operative discussion becomes reasonable. Change the interruption to sustained medication-free control and withdrawal/surveillance becomes reasonable.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting the interruption makes withdrawal plausible. Deleting duration removes the specific reason to postpone an otherwise plausible elective-surgery discussion. The preference supplies a genuine operative competitor; willingness to bridge limits that preference now.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone response case: no earlier scored node, correct answer, explanation or partial result supplies this decision. The entire header, update, exhibit and options were re-solved together.
gate.repairLog: One response to independent REVISE, version 2. Replaced untreated safe counts and three already-premature escalations with an actual treatment-response record. Duration now affects whether surgery is deferred; no exact dose or drug-failure threshold is invented. Within this response pass, replaced the paired-plan matrix after a component-frequency cue attack exposed majority-component convergence.

revisionDrafts.objective: Reconcile the missing vaccine and preserve its feasible preoperative interval.
revisionDrafts.stem: Which vaccination and operative-date plan should the clinic recommend for {patientName}'s elective splenectomy?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Visit and hospital booking
items.value: Clinic visit: November 11, 2026. Hospital splenectomy is booked for November 16, 2026 for chronic ITP. There is no current bleeding or urgent operative indication.

items.label: Verified vaccination extract
items.value: PCV20 was administered September 1, 2026. MenACWY and MenB records have been reconciled separately. The complete childhood and adult administration record contains no Hib entry.

choices.label: Give Hib November 11; operate November 25
choices.rationale: An adult without a Hib history needs the indicated dose; PCV20 does not call for an added PPSV23 dose. The later operative date provides the recommended preoperative lead time.
choices.temptation: Recognize the vaccine need but ignore the elective calendar.
choices.counterfactual: If the operation were urgent, the preferred elective vaccine interval would not by itself justify delaying necessary surgery.

choices.label: Give Hib November 11; operate November 16
choices.rationale: This selects the indicated vaccine but leaves only five days before an operation that can be deferred.
choices.temptation: Match the missing vaccine without checking the two actual dates.
choices.counterfactual: An urgent operative indication would change the delay decision; it is absent from this record.

choices.label: Give PPSV23 November 11; operate November 25
choices.rationale: The timing is compatible with elective preparation, but the administered PCV20 does not need PPSV23 completion and the Hib indication remains.
choices.temptation: Apply a PCV15 completion rule to a PCV20 record.
choices.counterfactual: With PCV15 given at the appropriate prior interval and a documented Hib dose already administered, PPSV23 rather than Hib could be indicated.

choices.label: Give PPSV23 November 11; operate November 16
choices.rationale: This combines the wrong pneumococcal completion inference with a short elective vaccine-to-operation interval.
choices.temptation: Treat every conjugate product as a two-vaccine sequence while retaining the booked date.
choices.counterfactual: A different record showing PPSV23 indicated plus a truly urgent operation would alter both components; neither circumstance is present.

revisionDrafts.explanation: Read the administered product before applying a completion rule: PCV20 does not require PPSV23. The adult Hib history establishes the indicated dose. November 25 is fourteen days after vaccination, whereas November 16 is five days later. For this deferrable elective operation, use the recommended preoperative lead time. Urgent splenectomy has a different timing balance.

reasoningSteps: Interpret the administration record to distinguish an indicated Hib dose from an unnecessary PCV20-to-PPSV23 completion dose.
Apply the preoperative lead-time recommendation to the fixed clinic and hospital dates.
gate.closestError: The closest error gives the correct Hib dose on the correct visit but retains the booked operation five days later.
gate.decidingObservation: The PCV product is 20, the Hib history is absent, and the nonurgent operation is booked five days after this fixed visit.
gate.consequence: An incorrect plan would expose this patient to an unnecessary intervention or defer indicated protection or disease-directed assessment.
gate.cueAttack: Neutral task names no vaccine. The four options form a balanced two-by-two comparison: each vaccine and each date occurs twice. All dates refer to the same visible encounter, not an undefined recovery date.
gate.stageAndCategory: One current decision stage: specific management plans with comparable scope; patient observations and rationale remain separated.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate; author estimate only, pending independent re-review. The nearest competitor is identified below rather than using rarity to claim difficulty.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Hib on November 11 with surgery November 25 wins. Replace the record with PCV15 at a valid completion interval and Hib already administered, and the vaccine component changes to PPSV23. Make the operation urgent and elective deferral no longer follows automatically.
gate.deletionTest: PCV20 is needed to reject the competing pneumococcal completion plan. Hib history identifies the relevant dose. Both dates and lack of urgency determine the calendar; nonspecific immune-response permission and ambiguous post-recovery reference dates were deleted.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone response case: no earlier scored node, correct answer, explanation or partial result supplies this decision. The entire header, update, exhibit and options were re-solved together.
gate.repairLog: One response to independent REVISE, version 2. Removed named-Hib task, unsupported broad immune-response permission and ambiguous fourth schedule. The closest competitor now gets the vaccine right and the calendar wrong.

revisionDrafts.objective: Use recovered production, ongoing hemolysis and functional/transfusion burden to reconsider elective splenectomy.
revisionDrafts.stem: Which longer-term plan should the clinic discuss with {patientName} after reviewing these hereditary-spherocytosis records?

choices.label: Begin elective splenectomy assessment
choices.rationale: The later reticulocyte course differs from the acute production arrest. Persistent hemolytic findings, transfusion burden and functional loss justify operative assessment rather than using the acute episode as a reason for indefinite delay.
choices.temptation: Continue treating an old mechanism after the observations have changed.
choices.counterfactual: If the later reticulocyte count remained near the acute low value, production recovery and evaluation would remain the immediate issue.

choices.label: Continue surveillance without splenectomy assessment
choices.rationale: Surveillance is reasonable for clinically mild disease, but the current record includes recurrent transfusion need and substantial functional impairment.
choices.temptation: Treat any post-illness follow-up as a reason to avoid revisiting disease-directed options.
choices.counterfactual: Stable hemoglobin without transfusions or functional limitation would favor surveillance rather than an operative assessment.

choices.label: Continue transfusion support pending reticulocyte recovery
choices.rationale: Transfusions can still be needed, but the high later reticulocyte counts do not support waiting for resolution of the earlier production arrest as the longer-term plan.
choices.temptation: Anchor on the very low reticulocyte count in the acute admission.
choices.counterfactual: Persistently suppressed reticulocytes after the acute illness would make production evaluation and supportive treatment the appropriate priority.

revisionDrafts.explanation: The later reticulocyte counts show a different process from the near-absent production during the febrile illness. Persistent anemia with a reticulocyte response and hemolytic markers, together with repeated transfusions and functional limitation, supports splenectomy assessment for the underlying HS. This is an assessment recommendation, not an unsupported ranking of total versus partial surgery.

reasoningSteps: Infer the change from the acute low-reticulocyte episode to later anemia with an active reticulocyte response and hemolytic markers.
Use continuing transfusion and functional burden to choose operative assessment rather than mild-disease surveillance or waiting for production recovery.
gate.closestError: The nearest competitor continues support while waiting for the reticulocyte recovery that the later raw counts already demonstrate.
gate.decidingObservation: Reticulocytes are now 13-15% while anemia, hemolytic markers, repeated transfusions and loss of usual function persist.
gate.consequence: An incorrect plan would expose this patient to an unnecessary intervention or defer indicated protection or disease-directed assessment.
gate.cueAttack: No current interpretation is supplied. All options are longer-term management plans; the weak glucocorticoid foil is removed. No earlier crisis-node feedback precedes this standalone version.
gate.stageAndCategory: One current decision stage: specific management plans with comparable scope; patient observations and rationale remain separated.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate; author estimate only, pending independent re-review. The nearest competitor is identified below rather than using rarity to claim difficulty.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Offer splenectomy assessment here. Keep later reticulocytes near 0.1% and supportive treatment with production evaluation wins. Replace the later course with stable hemoglobin, no transfusion need and normal function and surveillance wins.
gate.deletionTest: Serial counts replace the supplied production-recovered conclusion. The acute observation provides the competing mechanism; the later response changes it. Transfusion and functional burden distinguish the current course from mild HS.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone response case: no earlier scored node, correct answer, explanation or partial result supplies this decision. The entire header, update, exhibit and options were re-solved together.
gate.repairLog: One response to independent REVISE, version 2. Removed the production-recovered label, the ambiguous scheduled date and the steroid distractor. Split away from the parked acute timing node so its feedback cannot teach this decision.

revisionDrafts.objective: Recognize PIEZO1-associated dehydration as a different operative-risk disease from presumed HS.
revisionDrafts.stem: Which operative plan is appropriate for {patientName} after review of the new red-cell results?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Referral label
items.value: Chronic familial hemolytic anemia has been treated as hereditary spherocytosis; splenectomy was proposed for ongoing symptoms.

items.label: Specialist red-cell laboratory
items.value: Few stomatocytes and no dominant spherocyte population. Osmotic-gradient ektacytometry shows a left-shifted dehydrated profile.

items.label: Molecular result
items.value: A pathogenic gain-of-function PIEZO1 variant is identified.

choices.label: Withdraw the splenectomy plan and return to hematology
choices.rationale: The new findings support hereditary xerocytosis, whose limited splenic benefit and thrombotic risk differ from HS.
choices.temptation: Treat familial hemolysis as a single surgically responsive category.
choices.counterfactual: A supported HS diagnosis with severe clinical burden would restore a different operative discussion.

choices.label: Proceed with the planned total splenectomy
choices.rationale: The diagnosis underpinning the proposed benefit has changed; the new disease carries a different risk balance.
choices.temptation: Carry the referral label forward despite new mechanism evidence.
choices.counterfactual: True severe HS after complete assessment may justify surgery.

choices.label: Replace total splenectomy with partial splenectomy
choices.rationale: A smaller operation does not establish an evidence-supported solution to this disease-specific contraindication.
choices.temptation: Reduce operative extent without resolving the wrong indication.
choices.counterfactual: Partial removal is a separate option in selected HS cases with a real indication; it is not a proved workaround here.

revisionDrafts.explanation: The genetic and dehydration findings redirect the diagnosis toward hereditary xerocytosis. Do not carry the presumed-HS splenectomy plan forward or assume partial removal neutralizes the different thrombotic risk. Return to specialist hematology planning.

reasoningSteps: Integrate the dehydration phenotype with a pathogenic PIEZO1 gain-of-function result to reject the referral's HS premise.
Apply the distinct benefit/risk of that disorder to stop the planned splenic operation.
gate.closestError: Preserve a surgical plan by changing extent while ignoring a changed disease mechanism.
gate.decidingObservation: PIEZO1 result plus a dehydrated, nonspherocytic phenotype.
gate.consequence: A poorly beneficial operation with a different thrombotic hazard may occur.
gate.cueAttack: The neutral task permits retaining, changing or withdrawing the proposed operation. No grammatical presupposition of a change eliminates proceeding before the laboratory findings are interpreted.
gate.stageAndCategory: Revision of an existing operative plan.
gate.difficulty: Predicted hard stretch item, not verified common examination coverage. The difficulty includes specialist membrane-disorder recognition; clinician review remains required.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Withdraw the plan wins. A supported severe HS diagnosis changes the risk/benefit and supports a renewed operative discussion.
gate.deletionTest: The gene and phenotype must agree; symptoms establish why the initial proposal was plausible. No exact genetic variant or laboratory cutoff invented.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone clinic review of outside specialist testing; no additional diagnosis module or scored hematology companion required.
gate.repairLog: One response to REVISE, version 2: changed only the biased task, retained the supported diagnostic-to-operative-risk inference and marked this as stretch coverage.

revisionDrafts.objective: Use the recorded conjugate product to distinguish completed vaccination from a remaining polysaccharide dose.
revisionDrafts.stem: Which pneumococcal plan fits {patientName}'s reconciled administration record?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Risk history
items.value: Anatomic asplenia after splenectomy; no stem-cell transplant.

items.label: Hospital referral record
items.value: An unsigned PCV15 order remains on the referral medication list from November 2024.

items.label: Vaccination clinic record
items.value: The signed November 2024 administration entry identifies PCV20, including its lot and injection site. The PCV15 order is marked cancelled; there is no administration entry for it. No other pneumococcal doses appear in the reconciled record.

items.label: Current encounter
items.value: November 11, 2026.

choices.label: Give no dose at this visit
choices.rationale: The administered product was PCV20; the unadministered PCV15 order does not establish a different sequence. PCV20 is an endpoint under this schedule.
choices.temptation: Treat an order list as proof that the ordered product was administered.
choices.counterfactual: If the signed administration record instead showed PCV15 without later PPSV23, PPSV23 completion would be appropriate at this interval.

choices.label: Give PPSV23 at this visit
choices.rationale: This follows the PCV15 order instead of the documented PCV20 administration. The latter does not require PPSV23.
choices.temptation: Resolve a product discrepancy using the referral order rather than the administration record.
choices.counterfactual: A signed PCV15 administration record with no later completion would support PPSV23 at this visit.

choices.label: Give PCV20 at this visit
choices.rationale: There is a verified PCV20 administration already. The discrepancy does not make this an unknown conjugate-vaccine history.
choices.temptation: Treat disagreement between an order and administration record as absent vaccination.
choices.counterfactual: If the order had been cancelled and no pneumococcal conjugate dose had actually been administered, PCV20 would be an appropriate option.

revisionDrafts.explanation: Distinguish an ordered product from the administered product before applying its schedule. Here the signed record establishes PCV20, so the PCV15-to-PPSV23 completion rule does not apply. A verified PCV20 dose does not need another pneumococcal dose in this non-transplant record.

reasoningSteps: Resolve the order-versus-administration discrepancy using the actual administered product.
Apply the PCV20 endpoint rather than the PCV15 completion or unknown-history schedule.
gate.closestError: PPSV23 is a credible competitor if the resident follows the still-listed PCV15 order instead of the signed administration record.
gate.decidingObservation: The PCV15 entry was an unadministered cancelled order; the signed lot/site entry documents PCV20.
gate.consequence: An incorrect plan would expose this patient to an unnecessary intervention or defer indicated protection or disease-directed assessment.
gate.cueAttack: Three parallel current-visit dose plans. No option calls another dose redundant or a series completed in its visible label. This requires resolving an actual product/provenance discrepancy rather than adding unrelated completed vaccines.
gate.stageAndCategory: One current decision stage: specific management plans with comparable scope; patient observations and rationale remain separated.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate; author estimate only, pending independent re-review. The nearest competitor is identified below rather than using rarity to claim difficulty.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: No pneumococcal dose is due here. Change the signed administered product to PCV15 and PPSV23 becomes the completion choice at this two-year interval. Change it to no administered conjugate dose and PCV20 becomes appropriate.
gate.deletionTest: The discrepant order is needed for the credible PPSV23 error; the administration record resolves it. The encounter date anchors the competing completion interval. Asplenia gives the surgical prevention context; transplant would be a different schedule.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone response case: no earlier scored node, correct answer, explanation or partial result supplies this decision. The entire header, update, exhibit and options were re-solved together.
gate.repairLog: One response to independent REVISE, version 2. Added a meaningful cancelled-order/signed-administration discrepancy and a date, while retaining the same pneumococcal endpoint concept. No invented special immune circumstance or focused-basic exception is claimed.

revisionDrafts.objective: Distinguish MenACWY coverage from a missing MenB primary course in an older asplenic adult.
revisionDrafts.stem: Which meningococcal vaccination plan fits {patientName}'s current record?

choices.label: Start a MenB primary series at this visit
choices.rationale: The entries describe ACWY vaccination, not serogroup-B protection. Asplenia supplies a risk-based MenB indication despite being outside the usual healthy-young-adult age range.
choices.temptation: Treat a meningococcal record as protection against every serogroup.
choices.counterfactual: If a full MenB course and a current MenB booster were documented as well, no MenB dose would be needed at this visit.

choices.label: Give a MenACWY booster at this visit
choices.rationale: The documented ACWY booster was only last year. Another ACWY dose does not address the separate serogroup-B indication.
choices.temptation: Assume any additional meningococcal protection should use the previously recorded vaccine type.
choices.counterfactual: If the last ACWY dose were at least five years ago while MenB protection was current, an ACWY booster would be the indicated action.

choices.label: Defer meningococcal vaccination at this visit
choices.rationale: Age does not remove the asplenia-related MenB indication. The existing ACWY course is not a substitute for that protection.
choices.temptation: Apply the healthy-young-adult age window or regard the ACWY record as comprehensive.
choices.counterfactual: With current ACWY and MenB primary/booster histories, deferring another dose at this visit would be appropriate.

revisionDrafts.explanation: The record contains an ACWY primary course and a recent ACWY booster, but those entries do not establish serogroup-B protection. Asplenia creates an ongoing risk-based MenB indication beyond the routine young-adult window. Start the indicated MenB primary series rather than repeating ACWY or treating age as a reason to defer.

reasoningSteps: Interpret the actual ACWY administration entries and dates as a different protection category from MenB.
Apply ongoing asplenia risk rather than the routine healthy-young-adult age window to the current vaccination decision.
gate.closestError: Defer vaccination is credible if the reader mistakes ACWY for comprehensive protection or applies the routine young-adult age window; another ACWY booster is the product-category error.
gate.decidingObservation: Every verified entry is MenACWY, its last dose was in 2025, and the 61-year-old patient remains asplenic.
gate.consequence: The wrong plan would leave indicated protection or infection control incomplete, or add an unnecessary intervention with its own burden.
gate.cueAttack: No pre-answer sentence names an absent MenB dose or calls the ACWY series adequate/completed. Neutral administration entries replace the review conclusions. None of the visible options explains its own redundancy.
gate.stageAndCategory: One current decision stage: three specific treatment or vaccination plans with comparable scope and neutral labels.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate; author estimate only pending independent re-review. Competition comes from interpreting the record, not a deliberately easy exception.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Begin MenB here. Add a valid MenB course with a recent booster and deferral wins. Instead make the ACWY booster more than five years old while MenB is current and ACWY booster wins.
gate.deletionTest: Age supplies the routine-versus-risk competitor. Asplenia changes that age-based decision. The complete administration extract is necessary to interpret category coverage, and the dates prevent another ACWY booster from being equally due.
gate.sequenceAudit: Self-contained single-node response case. There is no earlier answer or explanation to supply this decision; all necessary dated history and patient context appear here.
gate.repairLog: One response to independent REVISE, version 2. Removed the named missing-action cue and explicitly redundant ACWY label. Current guidance supplies the separate risk-based indication and booster interval; no exact product-dose schedule is guessed.

items.label: Referral list
items.value: The hospital discharge list carries a PCV20 order dated November 2024.

items.label: Actual administration
items.value: The vaccination clinic signed an administration entry for PCV15 in November 2024, with lot and injection-site documentation. The PCV20 order was cancelled without administration. These are the only pneumococcal entries in the reconciled hospital and clinic record.

choices.label: Give PPSV23 at this visit
choices.rationale: The actual administered product was PCV15 rather than the ordered PCV20. At this interval, complete the indicated sequence instead of treating the unadministered order as an endpoint.
choices.temptation: Apply a PCV20 endpoint to a different product that was actually administered.
choices.counterfactual: If the signed administration instead documented PCV20, no additional pneumococcal dose would be indicated in this record.

choices.label: Give PCV15 at this visit
choices.rationale: The signed PCV15 dose remains part of the record despite the extended interval. Repeating it does not address the indicated completion step.
choices.temptation: Treat an interrupted schedule as if its prior dose had been erased.
choices.counterfactual: If neither ordered nor substituted vaccine had actually been administered, PCV15 could be used to initiate a sequence with its later completion planned.

choices.label: Give no pneumococcal dose at this visit
choices.rationale: The cancelled PCV20 order cannot establish a completed PCV20 history. The actual PCV15 administration still calls for completion.
choices.temptation: Follow a referral list rather than the administered-product record.
choices.counterfactual: A verified PCV20 administration, or PCV15 followed by a documented valid PPSV23 dose, would support no additional dose now.

revisionDrafts.explanation: The administered vaccine, not the referral order, determines the sequence. PCV15 was given; PCV20 was not. The two-year gap does not invalidate the earlier dose or require a restart. Complete the PCV15 sequence with PPSV23 at this visit under the cited schedule.

reasoningSteps: Resolve the ordered-PCV20 versus administered-PCV15 discrepancy.
Apply completion rather than endpoint or restart logic at the fixed later encounter.
gate.closestError: The nearest competitor gives no dose by crediting the cancelled PCV20 order; repeating PCV15 represents the interrupted-series misconception.
gate.decidingObservation: The signed lot/site record documents PCV15, with no administered PCV20 or later pneumococcal dose, two years before this encounter.
gate.consequence: The wrong plan would leave indicated protection or infection control incomplete, or add an unnecessary intervention with its own burden.
gate.cueAttack: Parallel dose plans omit explanatory words such as restart, completed and redundant. The patient does not supply the misconception. An actual administration discrepancy replaces a mere list of named missing vaccines.
gate.stageAndCategory: One current decision stage: three specific treatment or vaccination plans with comparable scope and neutral labels.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate; author estimate only pending independent re-review. Competition comes from interpreting the record, not a deliberately easy exception.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: PPSV23 wins here. Change the actual administered product to PCV20 and no further dose wins. If the earlier event were an unadministered order with no actual conjugate dose, initiation with PCV15 could be appropriate.
gate.deletionTest: Both source records are needed to make the product discrepancy consequential. The fixed date establishes a valid completion interval. The patient restart question and broad no-contraindication permission were deleted.

revisionDrafts.objective: Distinguish maintenance boosting from restarting a complete primary course or ending risk-based vaccination.
revisionDrafts.stem: Which meningococcal dose should be given at {patientName}'s current follow-up visit?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Visit and risk state
items.value: November 11, 2026. Anatomic asplenia remains.

items.label: MenB administration record
items.value: Trumenba: January 10, 2020; March 10, 2020; July 10, 2020; July 10, 2021; November 10, 2023.

items.label: MenACWY administration record
items.value: MenACWY: January 10, 2020; March 10, 2020; November 10, 2025.

choices.label: Give one Trumenba dose at this visit
choices.rationale: The MenB course has reached a further booster interval, while the recent ACWY booster does not call for another ACWY dose. Continue the recorded MenB product.
choices.temptation: Treat all meningococcal booster schedules as sharing the same interval.
choices.counterfactual: If both ACWY and MenB boosters were due at the same visit, the compatible combined product could become an appropriate option.

choices.label: Give one Penbraya dose at this visit
choices.rationale: The combination contains the compatible MenB component, but CDC reserves combined dosing for a visit at which both ACWY and B doses are indicated. ACWY was boosted last year.
choices.temptation: Use broader combined protection whenever either meningococcal booster is due.
choices.counterfactual: With the same MenB history but an ACWY booster at least five years ago, combined dosing could be appropriate because both components would be due.

choices.label: Give one Bexsero dose at this visit
choices.rationale: MenB boosters continue the same product as the established course. A different MenB brand is not an interchangeable maintenance dose.
choices.temptation: Treat serogroup coverage as proof of product interchangeability.
choices.counterfactual: A Bexsero rather than Trumenba primary and booster history at these appropriate intervals would make Bexsero the maintenance product.

choices.label: Give no meningococcal dose at this visit
choices.rationale: The latest Trumenba dose was three years before the fixed encounter; ongoing asplenia calls for maintenance rather than indefinite deferral.
choices.temptation: Treat completion of a primary course or a recent ACWY dose as protection that eliminates further MenB maintenance.
choices.counterfactual: If the latest MenB booster, like ACWY, had been given one year before this encounter, neither booster would be due now and deferral would be the best offered plan.

revisionDrafts.explanation: Separate the two dated schedules. The last MenB dose was three years before this encounter, while the ACWY booster was one year earlier. MenB maintenance is due; ACWY is not. Use the same MenB product. A combined ACWY/B product is appropriate only when both components are indicated at the visit.

reasoningSteps: Interpret the raw administration dates as MenB maintenance due with ACWY maintenance not due.
Select the matching MenB product rather than a noninterchangeable brand or a combined product whose other component is not indicated now.
gate.closestError: Penbraya is the closest competitor because it includes the same MenB component but adds an ACWY component that is not due.
gate.decidingObservation: Three years have elapsed since the last Trumenba dose, but only one year since the ACWY booster.
gate.consequence: The wrong plan would leave indicated protection or infection control incomplete, or add an unnecessary intervention with its own burden.
gate.cueAttack: Four parallel current-visit dose plans. The recorded brand is legitimate evidence, but simple brand matching cannot reject a compatible combined product or establish that a dose is due. The no-dose option makes the MenB interval consequential; ACWY dates determine whether the combined product belongs in the same visit.
gate.stageAndCategory: One current vaccination decision: four specific current-visit dose plans with comparable scope and neutral labels.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate; author estimate only pending independent re-review. Competition comes from interpreting the record, not a deliberately easy exception.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: Trumenba wins here. If the latest MenB booster were in November 2025, both schedules would be current and the no-dose option would win. If the course used Bexsero, the maintenance product would change to Bexsero. If ACWY were also due, combined and compatible separate dosing could both be acceptable, requiring a rewritten single-best-answer item rather than a false unique key.
gate.deletionTest: The fixed encounter date prevents reliance on the filename or current real-world date. MenB dates establish maintenance rather than primary initiation. ACWY dates and MenB brand independently distinguish the two credible competitors.
gate.sequenceAudit: Self-contained single-node response case. There is no earlier answer or explanation to supply this decision; all necessary dated history and patient context appear here.
gate.repairLog: One response to independent REVISE, version 2. Added visible fixed dates and replaced extreme foils with a compatible combined-product error and a different-brand error. The counterfactual explicitly recognizes when combined and separate products would both be acceptable, rather than inventing unique superiority. A fourth no-dose competitor makes the fixed MenB interval necessary; no forced-dose assumption is needed.

revisionDrafts.objective: Integrate liquid collection anatomy and operative burden when selecting initial splenic abscess source control.
revisionDrafts.stem: At the first hospital treatment-planning point in these records, which treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s splenic infection?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Historical decision point
items.value: The founder is reviewing the first outside-hospital treatment discussion after diagnostic aspiration yielded pus. Blood and aspirate cultures identified the same organism. Culture-directed intravenous antibiotics have begun, but fever and left-upper-quadrant pain continue.

items.label: Examination at that time
items.value: The patient was alert, with blood pressure 124/72 mmHg and no vasopressor infusion. There was localized left-upper-quadrant tenderness without diffuse guarding.

items.label: CT at that time
items.value: One thick-walled subcapsular splenic cavity contains liquid, without internal septations. It abuts the lateral abdominal wall; no bowel lies between the cavity and that wall. The splenic capsule is intact, without free intraperitoneal fluid.

items.label: Respiratory history
items.value: Severe obstructive lung disease requiring home oxygen. A previous abdominal operation required prolonged postoperative ventilation.

choices.label: Arrange image-guided catheter drainage
choices.rationale: The liquid localized cavity and access observations support an initial percutaneous approach, and avoiding another burdensome operation matters with this respiratory history. Antibiotics continue as common background care.
choices.temptation: Choose the definitive operation without considering anatomy or operative burden.
choices.counterfactual: A changed record with multiple separated collections would shift the operative discussion, but additional-drainage feasibility would still need case-specific evaluation.

choices.label: Arrange hospital splenectomy
choices.rationale: Splenectomy is a real definitive treatment. Here the localized liquid target and substantial respiratory burden favor an initial less invasive attempt at the documented stable decision point.
choices.temptation: Apply a diagnosis-to-operation rule without comparing the actual collection and patient risk.
choices.counterfactual: If the collection were extensively septated and multiloculated rather than a single liquid cavity, the drainage rationale would weaken and operative source-control discussion would become stronger.

choices.label: Continue intravenous antibiotics
choices.rationale: Directed antibiotics remain necessary background care, but they leave a symptomatic undrained liquid focus. The record supports adding a procedure rather than retaining an unchanged treatment plan.
choices.temptation: Equate organism-directed treatment with control of the infected focus.
choices.counterfactual: If infection had resolved and imaging showed no residual collection, a new drainage procedure would no longer be indicated.

revisionDrafts.explanation: At this historical decision point, interpret the CT anatomy and the documented examination together. A localized liquid cavity without septations supports an image-guided drainage attempt, particularly with the prior respiratory operative burden. Continue the hospital antibiotics. This initial choice does not establish that every later complex collection can be drained, or that a specified number of antibiotic days defines failure.

reasoningSteps: Interpret the original examination and CT as a localized liquid infected target without the recorded features of a ruptured acute abdomen.
Balance that target and its access anatomy against the pulmonary operative burden to select initial catheter drainage.
gate.closestError: The nearest competitor is definitive splenectomy, a genuine treatment option whose burden must be weighed against this particular initial collection.
gate.decidingObservation: A single liquid unseptated wall-adjacent cavity, intact capsule and localized examination coexist with severe pulmonary operative burden.
gate.consequence: The wrong plan would leave indicated protection or infection control incomplete, or add an unnecessary intervention with its own burden.
gate.cueAttack: The task asks neutrally for a treatment plan, allowing medical and procedural alternatives at the same phase. Stability is supported by observations from the historical encounter rather than inferred from the later clinic visit. Removed the word drainage from the historical introduction so chronology does not repeat a word unique to the key.
gate.stageAndCategory: One current decision stage: three specific treatment or vaccination plans with comparable scope and neutral labels.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate; author estimate only pending independent re-review. Competition comes from interpreting the record, not a deliberately easy exception.
gate.bestAnswerAndCounterfactual: An initial catheter attempt wins here. Change the CT to extensively septated multiple collections and the basis for that single-catheter plan is removed; surgery becomes a stronger discussion, with feasibility and respiratory risk still requiring review. Change the record to resolved infection and no collection and a new procedure is not indicated.
gate.deletionTest: The explicit pre-drainage historical point resolves clinic-versus-hospital timing. Examination and capsule/free-fluid findings constrain the acute phase; cavity structure/access and respiratory history constrain the procedure choice. No arbitrary size, antibiotic duration or availability permission is supplied.
gate.sequenceAudit: Self-contained single-node response case. There is no earlier answer or explanation to supply this decision; all necessary dated history and patient context appear here.
gate.repairLog: One response to independent REVISE, version 2. Resolved the retrospective tense, procedure-preselecting task and missing historical stability/rupture context. The later repeat-drainage ranking is parked rather than generalized from multifocality. Single-guidance-source limitation remains explicit.

originalReview.title: Preoperative vaccines: response after rituximab
fairness: This requires distinguishing apparently sufficient vaccine-to-operation lead time from impaired response after recent anti-B-cell treatment, then choosing later revaccination rather than accepting or immediately repeating the doses. Both timelines matter.
Planning indicated revaccination after recovery is the best offered answer. The wording 'indicated' appropriately avoids declaring that every prior dose always needs repeating.

The B-cell finding is legitimate decision-critical evidence, not a pre-answer statement that the administered doses are ineffective. The diagnosis of chronic ITP is appropriate background for the management task.

The exact post-rituximab interval and vaccine-specific revaccination rules require clinician confirmation; no fresh schedule verification was performed. Detectable B cells alone should not be construed as a complete validated measure of vaccine competence. The explanation's stated interval and reassessment language limit that overreading.
Standalone chronology is coherent. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified offline.
suggestions: Optional precision in feedback: clarify that reassessment combines the verified treatment interval, immune status and vaccine-specific guidance; do not make a single peripheral B-cell result an automatic revaccination or surgery trigger.
Retain the distinction between vaccine administration, operative lead time and expected response; it supplies the genuine reasoning.

originalReview.title: Hospital record review: initial splenic abscess control
clarityIssues: The clinic presentation is retrospective, but 'should be recommended' sounds like a current treatment instruction. Explicitly identify the reviewed hospital decision point rather than leave the encounter's temporal perspective implicit.

cues.phrase: Which source-control plan
cues.why: The task preselects procedural source control while one choice is only continued antibiotic treatment. This removes a distractor by category and supplies the first management conclusion.

fairness: A single liquid unseptated collection with favorable access anatomy, persistent symptoms and substantial operative respiratory burden favors image-guided drainage among these choices.

Interpreting drainability and applying operative risk is a meaningful two-step comparison with splenectomy. The current antibiotic option, however, does not answer the same source-control task and is therefore weak.

The hospital record does not describe acute physiologic stability or rupture status. If either could alter the intended procedural ranking, add the relevant observed findings; do not assume the patient's later clinic attendance establishes prior hospital stability. This is a missing-context concern, not an assertion that this patient was unstable.
The explanation does not leak the later splenectomy choice and appropriately avoids a universal size threshold or guaranteed drainage success.
suggestions: Ask neutrally for the initial treatment plan at the specified hospital decision point, or compare three genuine procedural source-control approaches if three credible options exist.
Retain the anatomy and respiratory burden. Add only the observed acute safety information needed to make the chosen initial procedure unambiguous.
Keep the retrospective review frame short and consistent across both parts.

originalReview.title: Hospital record review: persistent multifocal splenic infection
clarityIssues: 'Repeat image-guided drainage' is ambiguous between replacing a catheter in the collapsed original cavity and placing additional catheters into separate locules. These are clinically different actions.

The later update does not carry forward the home-oxygen requirement or prior prolonged postoperative ventilation. Those major competing operative risks appear only in the first exhibit, so this node is weaker when presented independently.
The retrospective clinic frame and 'should now be discussed' again leave the historical decision point less direct than it could be.

cues.phrase: Which source-control plan should now be discussed
cues.why: As in the first part, the task's category discounts the antibiotics-only option before the record is interpreted.

fairness: The changed imaging and ongoing bacteremia require a new inference: successful drainage of one cavity does not establish control of the remaining splenic infection. That is consequential and distinct from the first decision.

Splenectomy discussion is reasonable, but multiple separate locules without a dominant cavity do not by themselves establish that additional image-guided drainage is infeasible. The original substantial pulmonary risk makes that distinction especially important.

The item needs a supported patient-specific basis for ranking surgery over additional drainage. This is clinical ranking uncertainty, not a confident claim that splenectomy is wrong or that additional drains must work.

The chronology is otherwise coherent: the original catheter is patent and its cavity collapsed, then separate foci persist. Prior feedback cautions that drainage may fail but does not directly supply the surgical answer.
suggestions: Define the drainage alternative precisely and supply the observed access/anatomic or actual procedural findings that make it less appropriate in this patient. Do not replace that evidence with an unsupported blanket statement that multifocal disease cannot be drained.
Carry the relevant operative-risk history into the update so the later node stands alone and actually weighs the earlier competing consideration.
Use a neutral next-treatment task or only genuine source-control options, then have the clinician resolve the exact surgical-versus-additional-drainage ranking.
